paragraphs.heading: The foundational verse
paragraphs.text: In 1 Peter 3:15, Peter wrote this: "But in your hearts, set apart Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you, to give a reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect." Oftentimes, when we're talking about things like apologetics, this verse is the foundational verse that everyone seems to cite. Why? Well, because it is in this verse that we get the idea of apologetics.

So Peter is asking us, or commanding us, to give a reason. He's saying, give an actual reason. Well, what does it mean to give a reason? In this context, it means to give a defense: to give some kind of defending idea about what you believe. This is actually the Greek word apologia, and that's where we get the idea of apologetics. It literally comes from the word apology. Now, we're not talking about apologizing for what I believe.

But imagine for a moment a courtroom scenario, where you were on the stand and you had to give a defense — you had to give a reason for your actions, a reason for what you believe, or a reason just for what you're doing. In the ancient world, the context that Peter is talking about here is a group of Christians who were being persecuted by the Roman government. Here, Peter is telling the believers to be prepared, to know why you believe what you believe, to be able to stand in a formal sense in this context and give a reason, give a defense, defend one's belief in something.

And we take this command that Peter gives the early Christians and we say, you know what, we have the exact same responsibility in our day. It's to be able to stand when the questions come and to be able to give a reason for what we believe and why we believe it. So essentially, this is what apologetics is, and this is what you and your students are going to embark on this coming year.

paragraphs.heading: Called and capable
paragraphs.text: But it's more than just making a defense. It's the idea that we are both called, but we're also called to be capable. See, it's more than just saying, "I have to give a defense." How are you going to give a defense? What do you know, that would let you stand there and tell somebody what you believe and why? So this is exactly what we start to see — and what your students are going to start to see — with Peter in the early stages of Acts.

If you look at what Peter says in Acts, we've got this guy who literally ran away at the crucifixion, but then all of a sudden, in Acts, is proclaiming what he has seen and heard. We see in Acts 4:20 Peter say, "We can do nothing but speak of the things that we have seen and heard." So there was just this massive, compelling nature in them to be able to speak about the things they had seen and heard.

paragraphs.heading: Is apologetics necessary?
paragraphs.text: Now, it is important to remember that some people might not really think that this idea of apologetics is all that necessary. In fact, some might even say it's dangerous, and they might even look to passages like 1 Corinthians chapter 2, where Paul gives this idea that it is not by human wisdom or human power that he comes to the Corinthian church — that he didn't come with wise and persuasive words. A lot of people will take this to mean that we don't argue and that we don't want to persuade people. But in context, that's not exactly what Paul is talking about.

So we are called to maturity. We're called to be able to give evidence. We'll see throughout this study that if you look at the life of Jesus, if you look at the life of Paul, if you look at the things that Peter did, all of them gave consistent and good reasons for what they believed and why they believed it. So what we're really asking students, right out of the gate here, is to consider that very question: Why do you believe what you believe, and can you discuss those beliefs intelligently? Why do you believe what you believe?

So you and your students are headed on a huge, huge journey here, and it starts with getting students to begin thinking about these kinds of spiritual conversations. Some of the material we're going to be talking about is pretty heavy. Some of the topics we're going to be dealing with are going to be very challenging, not only for you, but challenging for your students as well. So you want to create a certain kind of environment.

paragraphs.heading: Create a safe environment
paragraphs.text: Now, some of you may already have this environment in your groups and some of you may not, but I want to encourage you to create an environment that really fosters this key idea of being able to ask and answer questions. This might seem really, really simple — "Well, yes, of course my students can ask questions" — but you would be surprised at the number of students who just don't feel like they can ask any question. Not just the difficult question, but maybe the question that really questions their own faith, the question that invites in this idea of doubt.

Now, we're going to be dealing with doubt, but much later. So you have to be able to create an environment where your students feel like they can ask anything, where they feel welcome, where it's a safe place. But that doesn't mean that you have to have all of the answers, because let's be honest: you're not going to have all the answers. Your students ask great questions.

In all the years that I've been a Christian educator, I have seen some amazing questions — the kind that leave you standing there with your jaw dropped. I don't know what to say to that, because I never would have thought of that question, and I love those kinds of questions. Don't feel like you have to have all the answers.

But what goes even further than having all of the answers is being able to walk alongside a student and say, "Hey, listen, I don't know the answer, but let's you and me figure this out together." That's going to do exactly what our goal is. That's going to create a stronger relationship between you and your students, while at the same time figuring out the answer to their question.

paragraphs.heading: Resources to lean on
paragraphs.text: So use the resources that you have available to you inside your church. Possibly a school or a seminary that might be nearby. Friends and family of yours who may have a deeper understanding. But also use us. We're here at AwanaYM.org. We have a ton of resources and a library that we are continuing to build. Definitely check out Sean's website at SeanMcDowell.org — he's got a ton of resources. And if you are still stumped, you can even contact us directly, and we are happy to help you in any way that we can.

We are here to assist you in this journey, but I can't stress this enough: be sure that your small group leaders — and you, in terms of a large group, whatever it is that you have going on — make sure your students feel like they can do this, that they can ask anything. And it might start with you giving them some of the questions that even you have, in terms of figuring out what this looks like. So get ready, dive in, don't hold back.

And know that all of us here at the Home Office are praying for you, praying for each other and for other groups around the country that are on this journey with you, as we navigate together what this looks like, as we explore more deeply what it means to be believers in Christ — what that looks like, how do we defend it, and how do we guide our students so that when they graduate, when they move on to bigger and better things beyond your youth group, they are prepared to successfully engage their culture and further the Kingdom of God.

paragraphs.heading: Wandering in the dark
paragraphs.text: Several years ago, I was in a brand new apartment. I woke up in the middle of the night to do something — I don't remember what it was. As I went back to bed, I rammed my toe so hard into the bed frame that I ended up breaking my toe. I didn't know I had broken it until I woke up the next morning. It was black and blue, my whole foot was all messed up, and I limped around for days. The doctor told me there was nothing that could be done about it, because I had simply broken my toe. The bed wasn't new, but the apartment was. When I woke up, it was pitch black and I couldn't see a thing. Naturally, I was so disoriented — I didn't know where I was, I didn't know what was going on — that I forgot where the bed was, because I forgot where I was.

Growing up, in my younger days as an early baby Christian, that's about how I thought of faith. I thought of faith as wandering in the darkness, trying to figure something out, hoping I don't stub my toe and hoping I don't do something dumb. And in reality, in my life, I actually did stub my toe, to the point where I walked away for quite some time. As I came back to the church, I realized something: faith is not at all like wandering in the darkness. What I've discovered is that so many students still hold that belief — that faith is either attaching themselves to what their parents believe and simply going along with something, or literally wandering around in the darkness, hoping that what they believe is somehow true, and that somehow at the end of all things, when this life ends, they'll find out that it actually is true.

paragraphs.heading: What John says about faith
paragraphs.text: What's interesting, though, is that John says something at the very end of his gospel that starts to speak to us about what faith actually is. It's in John chapter 20, verses 30 and 31, and John says this: "Jesus did many other miracles, or miraculous signs, in the presence of his disciples, which are not recorded in this book, but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name."

What's interesting is what John says here: that these miraculous signs, all of these things John has recorded in his gospel, are there so that you might believe — we are given reasons. And what's fascinating about the gospel of John is the seven miraculous signs that John gives, starting with Jesus turning water into wine and then ending with that magnitude of a miracle, the raising of Lazarus. And then, if you want to include the eighth one, Jesus' own resurrection — time after time, John sets it up so that we see, increasing in measure, all these signs that Jesus is exactly who he says he is. This is what we want students to actually get: that biblical faith is trust based on evidence, and that translates into a deeper relationship.

paragraphs.heading: Trust grows a relationship
paragraphs.text: Think about the relationships that you have. You don't just blindly trust somebody you don't know, but the more you get to know somebody, the more you trust them. The more you trust them, the deeper that relationship starts to go. That's how relationships work, and it's no different with our relationship with Christ. The more we know who he is, the more we know about what's going on and what the gospel is, the more we can trust — and the more reason we have to trust in what God is doing through Christ. And the more that we do that, the deeper our relationship with him goes.

This is exactly why we start this lesson with the idea of your students' trust between friends. We want them to get that sense of what it looks like, because our best and deepest relationships are built on a sense of trust — a deep sense of trust. And we have that because that person has either continually provided reasons to trust them, or maybe not reasons to trust them. So we want our students to be able to see how that works.

paragraphs.heading: Hebrews 11 and certainty
paragraphs.text: What's even more fascinating, I think, is that when we start thinking about what faith is and how this works, we naturally find ourselves in Hebrews 11. Hebrews 11:1: "Now faith is being sure of what we hope for and certain of what we do not see. This is what the ancients were commended for." Then the writer of Hebrews goes through that huge wall of faith, all these people who had the right kind of faith. We use this verse as the foundational piece of what faith means: being sure of what we hope for and certain of what we do not see. Well, that word "certain" — the word actually means, or has with it, the idea of a foundation or a substructure.

So think of it this way: it's a basement. The idea the writer is talking about is the basement in your home. When you walk downstairs into your basement — if you have one, or if you've ever walked into a basement — you generally don't fear that the whole house is going to cave in on you. Because when you've walked down into a basement, it has these huge metal beams and these metal poles, and they're driven into the cement, into the ground, and the whole house is being held up by those beams and that basement. And when you walk downstairs, you don't think anything of it. Why? Because the house is built on a solid foundation. If the foundation in the house is cracked, the house is starting to be no good, and you can't really do anything in the house until you fix the foundation.

So that's what the writer is saying. It's so sure, so fundamental, that you can walk into a house and feel totally confident — so much so that you don't even think about it. That's what faith is. It's that foundational piece of what we do not see; it's assurance of it. And in fact, if you take it one step deeper, the root word comes from the idea of an idea, or of one who stands immovable. It cannot be moved at all. One who is so rock solid and so dug into a foundation that it can't be moved. That is what our faith is, and that's what we want students to be able to see.

paragraphs.heading: Why Jesus kept his wounds
paragraphs.text: Think about it for a second. I was just thinking about this the other day: why did Jesus keep his wounds? Why would Jesus — he's Jesus. He resurrects, and yet at the end of John's gospel, he shows Thomas his wounds. Thomas wants to see them. He wants to see for himself what it is that Jesus... Why? It's Jesus. He's resurrected. What more evidence do you need?

But Jesus keeps his wounds. I've always found that really fascinating — that out of all the things Jesus could have done, we'd be thinking, "Well, I'm going to fix these wounds, because why would I want to have these holes in my wrist and this gash in my side? Why would I want to keep those?" One more reason, even if it was just for Thomas. One more reason to show that this is who I am, and I've done exactly what I said I was going to do.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: So, faith. We want our students to really understand the deep roots of faith — that it's not wandering in the darkness, but that it's assurance and evidence of belief. So our small group time should be something where students can take a step back, think about it, and discuss with each other what it really means to have faith.

And I want your students to start — and you should encourage your students to start — thinking about, "Well, do I have my own faith, or am I still just believing what my parents believed, or what other people have told me to believe? Or am I starting now to believe things on my own, based on what I'm now discovering?" And that starts with asking your students: have they considered the evidence? Have they considered all of the tools that are in here, especially that God has given us, to figure out whether what Jesus did and what God is doing and the whole of salvation history is enough?

So what we're talking about is finding a space where students can start to make their faith their own. It's easy for us as leaders to stand up in front of a bunch of students and tell them about our faith, and read through Scripture, and give them an interpretation of what our faith looks like and what faith they ought to have based on our faith. But it's a whole different thing — and this is the thing we want you to start doing — to encourage students so that this transfer begins to happen: the transfer from what we're telling them to believe to what they believe based on the evidence they're discovering on their own.

We want you to create a space where students can invest, where they can pursue on their own, where they can go back to the idea of questions — where they can ask the right questions, or ask any questions for that matter — so that the evidence that's here in Scripture will come right off the page and into their lives. That's the kind of faith that sticks. That's the kind of faith they'll take with them to college. That's the kind of faith we want them to have. We don't want them to just accept what we're telling them; we want them to discover that what we're telling them is actually true.

So, three things to keep in mind. One: drive home the fact that biblical faith is not without evidence. Biblical faith is not without evidence. Number two: Jesus has taken significant time and energy to give us that evidence. And finally, number three: for students, considering the evidence opens the door to a much deeper and more meaningful relationship with the Creator of the world.

paragraphs.heading: Word of the year 2016
paragraphs.text: Every year, Oxford Dictionary puts out a word of the year. The word of the year for 2016 was this: post-truth. It's an adjective, defined as relating to or denoting circumstances in which objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief. So in other words, post-truth means that you don't really need to worry about objective facts, and that it's really about how you feel about something. You don't have to necessarily agree with objective truth, but your own subjective truth is much more valuable. Essentially, this is the word of the year. This is exactly what we're up against, or what our students are up against.

Every day that they walk into the classroom at school, every day that they interact with their friends and see media and movies and music and everything else that's on TV, this is what we're talking about. It's essentially relativism, the idea that objective truth no longer matters and no longer has any space in our heads to navigate our own reality. In other words, if I don't like objective reality, I can just completely ignore it and not worry about it, and create my own reality, my own truth. You can probably already start to imagine what kind of problems this is going to cause in your own mind and with your students.

This is also often why we as leaders will stand in front of our students and start talking about something that we think and we know is objectively true, especially what's based on Scripture, and there's a wall between what we're saying and our students. Oftentimes they're looking at what we're saying and thinking, "Well, wait a minute, that's what you think to be true. I don't accept that as true." Even though we're saying that this is objectively true, that this is absolutely true, they don't necessarily agree with it.

See, you and I probably accepted truth for what it is, even if we didn't like it. Okay, this is what truth is; this is the reality of the situation, or the reality of our environment, or the reality of our lives. We may not like it, but we accept it and we deal with it, or we change it, or whatever. Students will base their truth off of the reality that they create, because they're told that's exactly what you're allowed to do. But it's important that you help your students see truth for what it really is.

paragraphs.heading: Why this lesson matters
paragraphs.text: This lesson is so, so important as you continue to move forward, because you can't talk about the reality or the authority of Scripture. You can't talk about the reality of the resurrection. You can't talk about the existence of God. You can't talk about the problem of evil. You can't talk about really anything else that you're going to dive into until your students understand the nature of truth.

So truth is what corresponds with reality. When you think of truth, and when you help your students think of truth, help them navigate away from this idea of post-truth and remind them that truth is what is real, what is reality. Reality is really a thing that's independent of me, or you, or your students. It is what it is, regardless of whether we're interacting with it or not. More than just understanding truth and reality is the understanding that genuine freedom comes by living through truth. Because remember, we're talking about what it means to have faith, and we're talking about truth in that context. Our students want to be free. We want them to experience the freedom that is in Christ and that comes from understanding what truth is. And truth is what corresponds with reality.

paragraphs.heading: Coherent is not the same as true
paragraphs.text: Now, it might be really tempting for them to think, well, as long as it makes sense, or as long as it's practical, then that's fine. Then it can be true, right? It can be coherent. It can be practical. It can be whatever. As long as it makes sense to me, then it can be true. Well, that's not necessarily the case. If you think about it, there are lots of things that are coherent. Think about belief in things like Santa Claus, or the Easter Bunny, or the Tooth Fairy. When we're kids, those things make all the sense in the world. But we know that these things don't line up with reality. Parents may spend a lot of time making these things incredibly practical, and yet they don't line up with reality.

And so it might make sense for some other religious beliefs, or some other ideas that students may come across, that sound good, sound like they make sense, sound very practical. That doesn't mean they line up with reality. It might sound really nice to say all religions lead to the same place, or that all religions have some idea of truth to them. But then what do we do in John 14 when Jesus says, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. Nobody gets to the Father but by me"? Jesus is making an objective truth claim. So either that is true or it's not, and it doesn't matter what I think of it. Either what Jesus said is true or not; whether I interact with it or not, whether I believe in it or not, it's either true or it's false. That's what we call objective truth.

So if what Jesus is saying is true, that makes every other belief that contradicts belief in Jesus false. We want our students to be able to see that truth is so critically important to furthering their discussions on what it means to believe in Christianity. Students in small group are going to have a really good chance this week to discuss and explore how truth opens the door to a life of freedom. Because really, when we boil this down, understanding truth is more than just intellectually understanding what truth is. It's understanding it so that it leads them to freedom, so that they can be in Christ and can live the life that God has purposed for them.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of truth
paragraphs.text: So when we're thinking about truth, there are two kinds of truth that we're really talking about. I've talked a lot about the idea of objective truth, but there's also something we call subjective truth. So there's objective and subjective. Well, what's the difference? Oftentimes this is where our view of truth gets confused, because we mix these two up. So helping to understand these on your end, as well as helping your students to understand this, is going to be one of those things that helps take down that wall dividing you and your students, and helps them see exactly what it is that you're saying when you're talking about Scripture. So first, let's talk about the idea of subjective truth.

Well, what is the idea of subjective truth? If I say something like, "I love mint chocolate chip ice cream," but you like another flavor, chocolate let's say, is it true that I think mint chocolate chip ice cream is the best kind of ice cream? Well, of course it's true, because I think it. And is it true at the same time that if you think chocolate ice cream is the best kind of ice cream, that that is in fact a true statement? Well, of course it's a true statement, because you think it. See, these are subjective truth statements.

They're true because they're based on my experience and my experience only. So it doesn't matter. Two different things can both be equally true at the same time. Two different flavors of ice cream can both be true at the exact same time, because it's completely subjective. And if I'm not here to say it, then this truth statement doesn't matter anymore. So it's completely subjective.

paragraphs.heading: Objective truth
paragraphs.text: On the other side is the idea of objective truth. Now, objective truth has to do with the object. So if you think of it this way: subject, object. The truth statement here is about the subject, and the truth statement here is about the object. So if I'm talking about ice cream, I'm talking about how I feel about the ice cream. But here, if I'm talking about something like my shirt, if I told you that my shirt was blue, you'd tell me I'm wrong. Well, why? Because my shirt isn't blue. My shirt is green. If I told you my shirt is black or white or anything but the color that my shirt actually is, then I'm wrong.

It's completely independent of my opinion. It's completely independent of my experience. Even if I never bought the shirt and it's still on the rack at the store, the shirt is still the color that it is, until it ceases to be that shirt and that color. So it doesn't matter. It's based on the object, my shirt, not my opinion. This one is based on my opinion; I'm the subject. So that's the distinguishing feature.

The problem is that what we do is we lump religion over here. We lump Jesus on the side of subjective truth. And we say, well, I can believe in Jesus subjectively, because based on my experience I think it's true, and it doesn't matter what anybody else thinks. And it doesn't matter if you disagree, because somebody else can believe in something completely different and it be equally true. But now we go back to John 14. Jesus said something that is independent of me. He said something that is an objective truth statement, whether it's true or not. So that puts belief in Jesus on the objective side.

So when we're talking about Jesus, when we're talking about Christianity, when we're talking about the way in which the world works and God being creator and all the things that we're going to talk about for the rest of the year, we're talking about objective truth statements. They're either true or they're not. And we have to make sure our students understand that they're here. It's not a matter of opinion or experience. It's a matter of reality.

paragraphs.heading: Truth leads to freedom
paragraphs.text: So truth is what corresponds with reality, which then leads to freedom. This is what we want our students to see primarily this week: that understanding objective truth, understanding that truth is often objective, understanding that belief in Jesus is objective, is how it corresponds and lines up with reality. And understanding those things is what's going to lead your students to the feeling and the understanding and the experience of genuine freedom in Christ.

paragraphs.heading: Why talk about logic
paragraphs.text: Now you might be asking, why in the world are we talking about logic? Certainly it makes sense to talk about faith. Certainly it makes sense to talk about truth. But why would we take an entire week out, in a Bible study, to talk about something so strange as logic? Well, I think it starts with what the writer of Hebrews says in the last part of chapter 5 and the early part of chapter 6.

Anyone who lives on milk, still an infant, is not acquainted with the teaching about righteousness, but solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained themselves to distinguish good from evil. Therefore, let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity. Peter says much the same thing about leaving the idea of spiritual milk and moving on to maturity. Paul says, be transformed in the renewing of your minds, and put off the old self and put on the new self, imitate God, have a mind like Christ.

And even Jesus said we need to worship God with all of our heart, with all of our soul, with all of our mind, and with all of our strength. It's clear throughout Scripture that logic has a place, and that it is a tool that shouldn't be considered a threat. In fact, it's an incredibly useful tool. After all, Jesus said it — and in fact, you'll find in the Bible study this week that Jesus even demonstrated it.

paragraphs.heading: Reduce to absurdity
paragraphs.text: We'll see a couple of strange things throughout the study, and one of those things is this weird term you see in Latin, called reductio ad absurdum. I'll say that again: reductio ad absurdum. Essentially, it's just a fancy Latin word that means reduce to absurdity. It's that simple — and even that seems kind of confusing. So let me give you an example that should help you explain this kind of strange concept to your students.

When I was a kid, every so often I would skip school, and this one time in particular my dad caught me. So naturally he asked me, why did you skip school? I had this genius idea, this genius logic that I had come up with, and I told him, well, all my friends were doing it, so that's why I did it. That makes sense. That made perfect sense in my head, and I kind of stood there waiting for him to make a response. He didn't take very long before he said, well, if all of your friends jumped off a bridge, would you too?

Essentially, what my dad was doing, whether he realized it or not, was taking my argument and drawing it out to its natural conclusion, which is absurd. And that's essentially what reductio ad absurdum is telling us. And when we see Matthew 22, that's Jesus engaging in the same sort of logical analysis in his confrontation with the Pharisees. So instead of fearing logic, our goal is to get students to embrace logic, and actually to get them to understand that logic is a vital tool in the search for truth.

paragraphs.heading: Logic in the search for truth
paragraphs.text: Remember what we're doing here throughout this process — we talked about this when we talked about truth: students are looking for what is true. We want students, at the end of this process, to be able to look truth squarely in the face and actually see Jesus. So logic is going to help them get to that point. In their intro experience, we want them first to actually see that in their relationships. Students are using logic in their relationships to search for truth in those relationships, and we want them to do the same thing with Jesus.

paragraphs.heading: Paul reasoned from Scripture
paragraphs.text: So take Paul, for example. If you look through Acts — whether Paul's in Corinth, whether he's in Ephesus, whether Paul's in Thessalonica or in Athens — what you see is that Paul is constantly using logic. He's reasoning from the Scriptures, helping them understand who Jesus is, what he's all about, and what salvation means. Essentially, Paul uses logic through and through in almost every single one of his arguments as he's traveling on his missionary journeys. So the idea is that we want to invite students into a space where they can be curious, where they can not only ask the questions but logically think through these things and add an intellectual piece to their faith.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: As you dive into small group, you're going to ask what looks like a really simple question: should faith make sense? That's kind of tricky, right? There's a little bit going on here that we need to address, because there's so much about Jesus that does not seem to make sense. There's so much about our faith that doesn't seem to make sense sometimes. But as we think through it, as we use logic, as we actually engage intellectually with our faith, there's a lot we can figure out, and God has given us the tools to do so.

And really, this is much of the Pharisees' problem. This is what we see from question one and from their motivation to get after Jesus. They just didn't really get it. But I want to take a second and really touch on question three, because it deals with potential arguments against Christianity and whether or not those arguments make sense.

Be careful here, but answer these honestly — talk about these honestly — because there are some arguments out there that sound pretty good, that seem to make some sense. But that doesn't mean they're logical, and it doesn't make them right. It just makes them additional arguments. Even so, a lot of them are worth talking about. Just make sure you gauge your students and know where they're at. If you don't think your students can handle it, that may be a question you want to sidestep for just a minute and then come back to when you think they're ready.

paragraphs.heading: Sending students out
paragraphs.text: So as students depart for this week, leave them with this question: what about your faith doesn't make sense to you? And challenge them with what it's going to take to spur them on to a mature faith. Because remember, Jesus calls us all to clear and careful thinking — the same kind of thinking that Jesus demonstrated.

paragraphs.heading: Getting my first glasses
paragraphs.text: When I was 15, I remember going to my mom and telling her that I was having a hard time seeing what was in front of me — I was having a hard time seeing the board. I didn't think much of it — I just didn't think much of it. But I realized that sitting in the back of class, where I like to sit, I couldn't see anything. Then it got serious when I started to drive and realized that there were signs I thought I should be able to see, or that my friends had told me about, that I wasn't seeing. Something wasn't right. So I went to the doctors — I went to the eye doctor — and they did all the little checks.

They put the little thing on your face and do all the dialing, and you read the lines and the letters and all that kind of stuff, and I didn't think much of it. They told me to flip the lenses and say which one was better, and we did the whole process of getting fitted for a pair of glasses. I thought nothing of it — until the day I walked in and picked them up. I picked them up and looked at them, and for the first time I put glasses on, and all of a sudden the world completely changed. Things were sharper. I could see things across the room that I didn't even know existed. My entire perception, my entire reality, really started to change, because now I could actually see the way I was supposed to see.

paragraphs.heading: What a worldview is
paragraphs.text: We're talking about worldviews. The most simplistic way to see it and understand it is this: you look at the world through a set of lenses, and how you look through those lenses dictates how you see the world. Worldview — how I view the world. But worldviews are more than that, and what you should now start to see through the worldview questions that were introduced is that worldviews are foundational. They are life-shaping questions about reality. It's not just the pair of glasses I'm looking through to see the world; it's literally how I'm interpreting it and how I'm living as a result of that view. Your students should see very quickly, through some of the activities in the Bible study, that a biblical worldview has a profound impact on how we live.

So this week I want you to keep three really important things in mind as you work through this lesson. We've talked about things like what apologetics is, and we've talked about what faith is. We've talked about what truth is. We've talked about logic. We've laid this foundation so that you can continue to move through this study. But now we need students to really understand what it means to see the world through a particular lens. And we don't just want them to see the world through the Christian lens. We want them to understand the world through a couple of other popular ways of seeing: naturalism and pantheism.

Then we're going to talk about what it looks like from a monotheistic worldview, because the way in which other people see the world is going to vastly, widely influence how your students start to see the world. When people who see the world differently are involved in making movies and writing music and doing art and making TV shows and writing books and everything else, that worldview is going to get communicated to your students. So they need to start to be able to see that. But before we can start into all of that, there are three really important things I want you to keep in mind, because some things are going to come up here that are going to be pretty impactful.

paragraphs.heading: Don't assume a biblical worldview
paragraphs.text: Number one: don't assume your students have a biblical worldview. If your group is a typical youth group where most of them call themselves Christians — where the majority are Christians — you might automatically assume that your students have a Christian worldview or a biblical worldview. That may not necessarily be the case. You're going to discover that your students have some inconsistencies and some contradictions in their worldview. In fact, worldviews are often — if you can imagine going to a buffet restaurant — worldviews are often like that now.

I mean, think about all the information we have. Think about what's available to our students via the internet: as soon as they want to know something, what do we ask? We ask Google, we ask Siri, we ask our questions over the internet to figure out the answers, rather than going to a library and looking at a book and considering the source. We just ask, and we look at the top five views on Google, and we go with it. Our students have more information available to them than at any other time in history.

So what happens is that students have what I call a buffet worldview. You walk into a restaurant that has a buffet, grab a plate, and you just start taking food that looks good; you just start grabbing whatever you want. Then when you're done with that, you get rid of that plate, you go back to the buffet, and you grab different stuff that looked good the next time — or maybe you go back and grab seconds of the stuff you really liked. But you grab it all together, and you eat at a very low, discounted price.

So you may automatically think that they have a biblical worldview, because somewhere along that buffet there are pieces of Christianity, pieces of Scripture in their worldview. But then, as you explore deeper — especially your small group leaders, as they explore deeper, get into more conversations, and build deeper relationships with those students — they're going to discover that there are some significant inconsistencies.

Now, don't panic. That's okay, because as we move through this process we'll hopefully iron out those inconsistencies and help them and guide them through a more consistent worldview. That's what the actual worldview questions are designed to do. By asking those four questions, it draws out what they think, but it also reveals the flaws in their thinking in a nice, gentle, respectful way. So make sure you encourage your students to answer honestly — and hopefully you've created that environment already. We don't want the answers they think we want to hear; we want their actual answers, whatever they may be. So don't freak out if you hear something that you totally did not expect.

paragraphs.heading: Coherent and consistent
paragraphs.text: Number two: worldviews have to be coherent and consistent. Even though the buffet sounds really good and it works for some — or at least it seems like it works for some — it doesn't, and over time that will cause problems. That's why you go back for seconds and take different things: it's the search to figure out the best possible combination, and that doesn't work. So throughout this process we're going to be helping students understand that this is what makes Christianity so compelling — it is entirely coherent and it is entirely consistent.

paragraphs.heading: Change takes time
paragraphs.text: And finally, don't expect students to change their worldview right away. Just because you see that they have a different worldview, or that they have inconsistencies in their worldview, or that there are some questions in their worldview, and you present the Christian worldview — even at the end of these 32 weeks — don't expect them to just go, "Oh, I'm going to put on a whole new pair of glasses and see the world totally differently." It doesn't work that way. In fact, it doesn't work that way at all. Changing how we see the world is not as easy as changing the prescription on a pair of glasses. It's a huge, huge adjustment.

In fact, it is sometimes so big that it causes discomfort and it causes anxiety, because to change how you see the world is to change almost your entire reality — how you understand things, how you answer the big questions in life, and how you interact with people. That's a lot of change. So be patient with your students. Walk alongside them. Help them figure it all out.

paragraphs.heading: Looking back over four weeks
paragraphs.text: Over the last several weeks, we've challenged you with a lot of adjustments that you need to make within the context of your group. We've talked about the idea of building relationships being the most important thing — not just the relationship between your students and Christ, but your relationships between you and your students, and that there needs to be that sense of trust built. We've also talked about the idea of really just fostering a community where questions and doubt are welcomed.

We've talked about this idea of worldviews and what this looks like, and about being patient with your students in determining what their worldview actually is, and not being surprised if somehow their worldview doesn't quite line up with what you thought. And we've even talked about how to get rid of that barrier wall between what you're talking about in terms of objective truth and their view of truth, in the very postmodern, relativistic, post-truth kind of world that they're consistently exposed to in school and in media and whatnot. That's a lot. That's a lot to take in over the course of four weeks.

paragraphs.heading: Take the pulse of your group
paragraphs.text: So now would be a really, really good time, if you haven't done so already, to check in with your small group leaders and check in with your other leaders to see how these things are going — to make sure that the community is starting to coalesce together, and that students feel like they can ask the questions. Check in with some of your key students who have the pulse of the youth group, to get a feel for where everybody is and whether you are accomplishing these goals. It might look to you like you are, but don't be surprised if there's a little bit of angst and a little bit of struggle. And don't panic either if it's not happening just yet.

The important thing right now is to keep your hand on the pulse of your group, so that you can navigate it as you go and so that you are increasing that level of trust and increasing the students' ability to ask the tough questions. You might suddenly fall back into old questions that were asked in different lessons, because now students finally feel like they can ask that particular question, or answer that particular question that we're asking of them. So just be ready for it. Check in with your small group leaders, check in with a couple of students to figure out where everything is, and then strategize as to how you might move forward.

paragraphs.heading: Three things to remember
paragraphs.text: But remember, when we're talking about worldviews, the three things you need to keep in mind are these: your students may not necessarily have the biblical worldview that you think they have; their worldview needs to not be a buffet, but coherent and consistent; and don't expect them to change it right away. Be patient — and I think that's probably the most important piece, to be patient with them. Pray with them. Continue to walk alongside them to help them understand truth and how it fits in, and how truth is going to change their reality, and how understanding Scripture and their understanding of truth is going to actually change their worldview slowly, but also profoundly.

paragraphs.heading: Why Exodus 6
paragraphs.text: One of my favorite passages in Scripture is Exodus 6. Why Exodus 6? Well, believe it or not, it's not because of Moses. And it's not because Moses is on the brink of the Israelites leaving Egypt, or because of this really cool escape plan that Moses is going to lead the nation of Israel on. No, believe it or not, here's why: because we discover something about God that we did not previously know, from the very beginning of Scripture all the way up to now.

In verse one of chapter six, the Lord said to Moses, "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Because of my mighty hand, he will let them go; because of my mighty hand, he will drive them out of his country." God also said to Moses, "I am the Lord. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty. But by my name, the Lord, I did not make myself known to them."

"I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, where they lived as aliens. Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered my covenant." I love this passage, because this is where we start to see God in a different light — as more than just this idea of God Almighty.

paragraphs.heading: The personal nature of God
paragraphs.text: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob saw God as God Almighty. All that means is the God who is better than every other god, the Creator God, just this person up here. Now, there is some relational stuff going on with those three, but not in the same way that we see it with Moses. He makes the covenant, but here he remembers the covenant, and the covenant is becoming more of a reality than it was before. This is where we start to see the personal nature of God.

And that is incredibly important when we start talking about monotheism, because we're not just talking about the fact that a singular God exists. We're talking about something slightly more than that. We talked about naturalism, the dominant view of the West. We talked about pantheism, the dominant view of the East. We talked about the conversions of the two and how they don't work on the buffet. We talked about all of those things. Monotheism really is the view that God has made himself known — that God has made himself known to us in a very personal and very real way.

paragraphs.heading: Before we go any further
paragraphs.text: But before we make a case for Christianity being true, before we go any further — we've talked about what truth is, and about logic and faith and apologetics. We've talked about worldviews, and we've talked about naturalism. We've talked about pantheism. Before we go any further — before we talk about the resurrection, and before we talk about Scripture, and before we talk about how God has made himself known — we need to be able to show that there is a single, personal, all-powerful creator.

paragraphs.heading: Monotheism as a worldview
paragraphs.text: So I want to make something really clear here. We're talking about monotheism as a worldview, and within that worldview you have other religions as well. You have Judaism, you have Christianity, but you also have Islam. When we're talking about the buffet of a bunch of worldviews, and when we're talking about monotheism, we're saying: listen, we're going to put the buffet aside, and we're going to order off a menu and get the actual dish that we know is the best possible dish, the one that satisfies us the most and gives us the proper nutrients.

In other words, the worldview that is most consistent, the worldview that is most coherent, and the worldview that speaks to reality the best. Next week and moving forward, we're going to talk specifically about why Christianity, within the framework of monotheism, is true, and the rest of them will go away. But for this right now, we're just talking about monotheism in general.

We're talking about the idea of a loving, personal God. When we talked about pantheism, we talked about the idea that there needs to be some kind of distinction. So we're going to take that distinction and take it one step further, and talk specifically about the idea of a personal, caring God. But I could take that even one step further. If you go back to Exodus 6 and look at what God says, he says, "I am the Lord. I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty." He appeared to them in one way.

paragraphs.heading: A God who redeems
paragraphs.text: But by himself, by his name, the Lord — this is again going back to the idea of Yahweh, I am who I am, the name of God, the utter holiness of God, the other-than-ness of God. God takes who he is a step further in front of Moses and says, I am more than just God Almighty over everything else. I am who I am, Yahweh. That kind of describes what this looks like, and we can add into our focus the idea of a God who redeems.

He is a God who is not just out there creating things and leaving it alone. We're talking about a God who is actively engaged in history, redeeming and pursuing his own creation, which is made in his image. He is chasing after us, even after we screwed it up. He is chasing us down, drawing us back to him, because of his love for us. That's pretty profound. That sets us up for what Jesus does. That sets us up for belief in the Holy Spirit. That sets us up for the belief in the Trinity that gives us a better understanding of who God is, as we move into what this idea of monotheism actually looks like.

paragraphs.heading: Back to your tables
paragraphs.text: So we've had you take your students — especially in small groups, and working through the Bible study in large group — and really get a feel for how naturalism and how pantheism have infiltrated and influenced our current culture. Now I want you to back out of that for a second and return to tables. I want you to explore with your students how looking at the world through the eyes of a monotheistic worldview could actually influence the culture.

Because ultimately, as Christians, we are called to get into our culture and impact our culture for the gospel. So what does that look like? How then does your worldview change? Even for your students who maybe don't see the world through a monotheistic worldview just yet, encourage them to take a step back, and ask them: what would it look like if I viewed the world that way?

What would it look like if I saw God as one God; more than one God, as a personal God; more than just a personal God, as one who cares and is actually pursuing me individually? How would that change your students' lives? How would that change their thoughts on morality? How would that change their thoughts on justice? How would that change their thoughts on love, and on their relationships with their friends and their family? How would it even change how they function at school? How would their entire lives change if they thought that way? So have them explore what that looks like, and encourage them to try it out and see what happens. And then, as we continue to move forward, we'll be building the case that within the monotheistic framework, Christianity represents absolute truth.

paragraphs.heading: Why pantheism matters
paragraphs.text: If naturalism is the dominant view of the West, pantheism is the dominant view of the East. Pantheism is interesting, and it may seem like much of pantheistic thought is far from your students. Even though it largely dominates Eastern culture, from Hindus to Buddhists and a bunch of others in that part of the world, it has made its way to the West — and in a really strange way. So you might think, for your youth group: why are we talking about pantheism? Why are we bothering with this? That's another part of the world, and I'm not taking my kids on a mission trip over there, so do I really need to spend an entire week dedicated to this sort of Eastern thought?

Well, do you like Star Wars? Have you ever heard of karma, meditation, even yoga? All of these things come from pantheistic thought, or a pantheistic worldview. So naturally, we cannot ignore its influence. We have to address it, we have to discuss it, and we have to get our students to understand what it exactly is, so that they can identify it and navigate through it successfully.

paragraphs.heading: What pantheism teaches
paragraphs.text: So what is pantheism? What are we talking about? Essentially, think of it this way: the idea of God — and I'm going to write God with a small g — is in all. Now, you can even say, more specifically, God is all. In Christianity we talk about the idea of the Holy Spirit being within us, right? So God is in us, and that's sort of the idea. Jesus comes, Jesus goes, He sends the Spirit, and the Spirit dwells within us. We have this idea of God in us — not just God with us, but God in us. Okay, that's great, but that's not the same thing when we're talking about pantheism. We're talking about the idea that God is literally part of everything.

So in a pantheistic way, God would be in me just as much as in the camera that I'm speaking to, as this table, as this Bible, as this marker, as this whiteboard, rocks, trees — pretty much all of it. All of nature is part of the divine. It's all part of who God is. It's all part of this divine sort of idea of the universe that's all combined into one. There's a divine spark in everything. That's essentially what pantheism teaches. So that's where we get this idea of essence, or force. When we talk about Star Wars, the idea of "may the force be with you" — that's the same kind of idea. It's a divine essence that's part of this. We can call it a force. There's something going on behind the scenes in everything else.

paragraphs.heading: The key idea of distinction
paragraphs.text: So God is present everywhere. It defines life now, it defines life later, it defines relationships, it defines everything — how we see and relate to God. But the key I want you to get here is the idea of distinction, and this is going to be important as you move forward. If naturalism is saying there's no God at all, pantheism is saying, well, there is God, but God is not distinct from anything that's created. God is a part of creation, He's a part of you and me; there's just no distinction. There's no God and us. There's just everything all together. So for pantheism, there is no distinction at all. Keep that in the back of your mind, especially as we move to next week when we talk about monotheism. That's going to be really, really important.

paragraphs.heading: Paul at the Areopagus
paragraphs.text: In our Bible study portion, we talk about Paul. We talk about Paul's interaction at the Areopagus on Mars Hill, and we talk about his interaction between the Epicureans and the Stoics. What's interesting is that these Stoics actually believed much of the same kinds of things that modern-day pantheism believes — that idea that God is somehow packed into every little piece of our world. And what Paul does is help them see that there is a distinction between the two: that God is here and we are here. That there's a separation. That although He's personal, although He's right here with us, He's distinct and other than us. And that's incredibly important.

Because what this does — the loss of distinction — is actually what leads us to the root of all sin, right? Of creating God, or creating idols that are a substitute for God. If you say that there's no distinction, then all of these things are just as divine as God. So I can worship rocks and trees and everything else. It's not any different if we don't have some kind of distinction. So it drives us right back to the root of our sin. It drives us right back to idolatry.

paragraphs.heading: Pantheism in Western culture
paragraphs.text: Your students probably won't see it right away, but you need to help them begin to see how Western culture has actually embraced a lot of pantheistic ideas about God and creation. Again, let's go back to the buffet. It's super easy for us to say, "Wow, that sounds really cool," because I can see how beautiful creation is and want to make that into a God-like thing. Or I can treat somebody, or an activity, that way — or I can find a center in myself and be that kind of person and elevate myself to a God-like stature. That sounds really cool.

And along the buffet line, it sounds like I can say, well, if I care about people, I can elevate them to that same status too. So I like justice; that seems to speak to some of my morality. Again, you start to go back to that buffet and start to piece things together. But when we put them all together, we realize once again that this isn't coherent and it isn't consistent.

paragraphs.heading: Speak truth in love
paragraphs.text: Now, one quick word of note here that I want to make sure we're clear on. If you're doing everything really, really well, chances are you have some students who are either seeking or maybe skeptical, who have some questions and are curious. And as we're talking about other worldviews — whether they believe these things specifically or not — you want to be careful that we don't offend. We want to be careful that we speak truth, that we do so in love, but that we help them understand that these things are terribly inconsistent and they don't work.

But we need to do it without making fun of it. We need to do it without making light of it. Because when we're talking about worldviews, as we talked about a few weeks ago, these things are ingrained in us and they are embedded in us, and to change is a huge, monumental change, and it can often, like we said, create some anxiety. So the last thing we want to do is invite non-believing students, invite our seekers and our skeptics, into our youth space and say, "Come with your questions, come with your curiosity, and we'll help you navigate — and we're going to accept you," but at the same time make light of or make fun of other worldviews. That's not going to work.

This is a very popular worldview. So is naturalism. There are some really, really smart people who have said some really, really intelligent things about these worldviews. Now, that doesn't make them true, but we have to respect what they believe and speak to how it does not line up with reality and how it does not line up with truth — but do so in love.

paragraphs.heading: Remember this
paragraphs.text: So remember: pantheism says God is all. God is in everything and a part of everything — the rocks, the trees, everything — and it's a divine force. And essentially, the key word here is that there is no distinction between God and creation, between creator and creation. Not only does this lead to the idea of idolatry — if we don't have the distinction, what does that make God? The very fact that we call Him God means that He is completely distinct, completely other than us, and completely holy.

And the idea is this: if God is here and completely other than me, then I have a standard to look to, so I understand what's right and what's wrong. I understand what's just and unjust. I understand the idea of love versus hate. Putting God outside of myself and making God completely distinct helps us navigate reality in a way that makes sense. We have to have some kind of distinction. It's God who is other than, God who is holy, God who is supreme creator over all. And it's in Him that we live and move and have our being.

paragraphs.heading: Which worldviews to cover
paragraphs.text: We've talked about what worldviews are, but what worldviews should we actually talk about? What worldviews are your students most exposed to? There are a lot of them. We're only going to touch on a couple of the most popular worldviews, and we're going to talk about some of the more dominant ones, as well as what a biblical worldview starts to look like. But the first one we're going to talk about is the idea of naturalism.

paragraphs.heading: What naturalism teaches
paragraphs.text: You can probably tell right out of the gate that the idea of naturalism has the idea of nature in it. Think of your senses. Think of the five senses that you have — what you can taste, touch, smell, and feel. Naturalism teaches that only those things are what constitutes reality, and there we're back to that word again. What is reality? When we're talking about these other worldviews, they're doing the same thing that we're trying to do: trying to talk about what is reality and what is truth. How do we interpret these things in light of what naturalism actually is? Those who believe in naturalism are trying to take the five senses and interpret reality and dictate what is true based on those factors. That's essentially what they're doing.

And this really — if you think about your students, especially those in public schools — this is exactly what they're being exposed to every day of the week. It's this idea of naturalism, especially for those students who are in STEM research type classes: science, math, et cetera, technology, those kinds of things. Because the sciences are very much focused on the idea of what we can observe, what we can see, what we can touch, what we can taste, what we can feel. Those kinds of things.

But also, what they're trying to do is not only figure out reality and truth, but they're trying to figure out meaning. Naturally, life has meaning. And this is where it gets a little bit tricky. The naturalism point of view, the naturalism worldview, is trying to figure out, well, what does it mean to have meaning in life? That's sort of sticky, because naturalism actually can't do that. From the viewpoint of naturalism, you're being told that any meaning in life has to be found through science. So science is the only one that can determine what kind of meaning there is. But science can only take us through the natural world. It doesn't consider anything else. And we'll get to more of that in a second.

paragraphs.heading: Why naturalism can't work
paragraphs.text: But what I want you to get is that this lesson is more than just understanding what naturalism is. It's being able to see that it can't work. And what we want our students to be able to determine is that they're not going to get away from it, because it's the dominant view of Western culture — but to be able to see things through it and interpret things in light of it, and to understand that naturalism might be trying to do these things, and might be trying to explain meaning through science and the natural world, the natural order of things and all that, but at the end of the day it doesn't really work. Why?

Well, because naturalism is most closely associated with the idea of atheism, which means no God, it cannot explain two fundamental questions. It can't explain the universe in terms of how, and it can't explain things in terms of why. Now, science is trying to do this. Science is trying to figure out how the universe was created, and how things got here, and how it is that we're all here. But science can't do this. It can't determine why. Is it just random? If it's random, why is it random? We could keep asking that why question over and over and over again.

And to dig a little bit deeper, it also can't do things like determine justice, love, morality. How do we determine those things? How do we bring up the reality that there is justice in the world? How do we bring up the reality that two people love each other, and that we should have love for our fellow humans and humankind? Why is killing somebody else wrong, even if it might benefit me? Why is stealing wrong? Why do we understand some morals to be universal for all cultures, of all people, of all time? Where do we get these things from?

See, this is where naturalism falls short, because when we're talking about things like justice, love, and morality, these aren't tangible things that I can grab hold of. These are not part of what I can taste, touch, smell, and physically feel. I can't do that with justice, necessarily. I can't really do that with morality. These are things that are deeper than what is on the surface, and they require a deeper explanation. So again, it's important for us to understand not only what naturalism actually is, but it's also important for us to understand that naturalism doesn't actually work.

paragraphs.heading: In your small groups
paragraphs.text: So in your small groups — especially in your small groups — make sure you take the time to allow students to discover and discuss how naturalism manifests itself in Western culture. What does that look like? Where do they see that in their schools and in their classes? It's not just evolutionary science and those kinds of things; it might be deeper than that. So get your students to have those discussions and get them to see beyond just the surface of what naturalism is, and have them start to analyze it in terms of reality and truth.

paragraphs.heading: Ecclesiastes and meaninglessness
paragraphs.text: One thing that's great about this Bible study is that we dive into Ecclesiastes and the things that Solomon wrote. I think he had this spot on, and it brings so much more to the surface when we consider this book in light of naturalism. He writes in the very, very beginning, right out of the gate: "Meaningless, meaningless, says the teacher, utterly meaningless. Everything is meaningless. What does man gain from all his labor at which he toils under the sun? Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." And what he's getting at through this whole book is the idea that without God putting meaning in life, life is meaningless — that all of our work and all of our efforts and everything that we stand for is meaningless.

So think about it. From a naturalistic perspective, without God, what is justice? Without God, what is love? Without God, what is morality? Why are we working, besides to make money? Why is there any nonprofit organization at all? Why do we care about clean water around the world? Why do we care about any of those things? Because from a naturalistic worldview, there is no meaning behind those things. There's no point to doing it, because we're all just going to die and be dust, and everything is going to go away, and we cease to exist.

But because we have the inclination to want to provide clean water, because we feel a sense of justice, because we understand certain morals are universal, because we love one another and we're called to love one another, we understand that there has got to be something greater beyond just the natural world. There has to be the supernatural world. There has to be a Creator God behind all of it.

paragraphs.heading: The buffet of worldviews
paragraphs.text: So we see so clearly — and I want your students to see this as well — that when we talk about naturalism, it might sound so easy and so simple. When we talk about that big buffet of worldviews, it might sound like, "Oh yeah, this idea works really well." But when they go down that buffet and they decide that, yeah, I believe in naturalism and I don't believe in God, but I believe in taking care of orphans and widows and providing clean water to children around the world who don't have it — those two things are now inconsistent. Those two things no longer make sense together. It's a great thing that you want to provide that for those people, but why do you want to do that?

So this goes back to what we talked about last week, with the idea that it has to be consistent. So if you're going to desire to take care of your fellow man and take care of people who can't take care of themselves, if you have that sense of justice and you have that sense of morality — why? Again, it takes us back to here, and naturalism can't answer that. So naturally, what we would say is that your worldview then needs to adjust. So help your students navigate this. This is a little bit tricky, and it requires some good discussions. Again, we'll keep reminding you: always, always, always let the discussion flow. Let students be honest about what they think, but challenge them in their thinking.

paragraphs.heading: Talking about science
paragraphs.text: All right, so now we get to talk about science. We get to talk about design. We get to talk about DNA. We get to talk about — well, let's be honest — we get to talk about a lot of things that several of us probably don't have a ton of expertise in. We talk about truth and logic and even what our faith is, and for most of us youth leaders, that's in our wheelhouse. But when we get into things like science, it gets a little bit more tricky.

You don't have to be an expert in this space. But I want you to pay attention to a couple of things and remember a couple of things as you work through these next several weeks focusing on things like science. Our students are taught this: if you ask your students, if you go into the public school classroom and look inside what their textbooks say and what teachers are saying, there is this sort of separation between things of faith and things of science. We're told that these things don't belong together.

paragraphs.heading: A seventh grade lesson
paragraphs.text: I remember even back when I was in seventh grade, many years ago, I was told something by my teacher. I looked up and saw this chart of a monkey suddenly becoming more and more, evolving into a man, and I remember looking at that and thinking, how can that be? I remember raising my hand and asking the question, saying this doesn't seem right. And I'll never forget what she said to me. It seemed to solve it for me. She said, "I get what you're saying, but that is religion and faith, and this is science." Even right there as a seventh grader, the dichotomy, the split, the two separate spheres of life were defined for me.

So for our students, that really is what's happening a lot. A lot of students are okay with that and they're comfortable with it, and that's fine. But the more we research, the more technologically advanced we become, the more STEM research and STEM-like subjects and careers become more popular and much more pursued by our students post-college, the more this separation is going to get defined. So it's crucially important that our students understand — and guess what? — these two things don't actually need to be separated. In fact, the more we discover through science, the more we actually are going to discover about God, and the more we discover how awesome he really is. Over these next couple of weeks, you're actually going to start to see that.

So don't feel like you have to know all the science. Don't run out to the library and get a bunch of science books and try to figure it all out. I've tried. Unless that's your thing — then knock yourself out. But for most of us, it's probably not a time thing we have, nor maybe even the ability. So don't worry about that. Focus on getting your students to see that these two worlds actually interconnect. I might even suggest that you find some of those students who are really, really amped up about science and love it — whether it be math, whether it be even computer technology, anything in biochemistry, anything in the science world — and get them switched on here and now. This is a great way to get some of those students engaged.

paragraphs.heading: Find a storyteller
paragraphs.text: So for this first week, I think one of the crucial parts of your gathering is going to be your storyteller. Really focus in on somebody who can connect science and faith. I would suggest you either find a university professor, find somebody in the science field, or find somebody who actually does biology or chemistry or some field in the sciences and is in your church congregation — somebody who can stand up and say to the students, "Here is how I connect these two things together. This is how I can see God when I'm looking through a telescope or a microscope. This is how I can see God in the field of math," or whatever it might be.

It's hard. And trust me, you're going to need to sit down and probably have a conversation with the person you'd like to do this, and make sure that they can comfortably make that connection. I've even talked to Christian educators who are math teachers and English teachers and science teachers who, even as their profession, have a really, really difficult time sometimes making those connections. I've done seminars with some teachers, helping them — especially math teachers, for some reason — to make that connection, so they can see their subject matter through a biblical lens.

So make sure you sit down with those people and help them see it if they don't already see it, but make sure that they can deliver that message to your students, because this is a crucial moment. If your students can see that from somebody else in your congregation who actually does some of the jobs that they might be pursuing down the road, that's a huge, huge win for you as you move forward in this study.

paragraphs.heading: Talk about school subjects
paragraphs.text: So in addition to the questions that we've provided for you, it would be a really, really good idea for you to talk specifically with your students about some of the school subjects and some of the things that they're actually learning in school. So whatever they happen to be learning at this particular time in their curriculum, have them talk about that. You might even have them bring in their textbooks.

Have them talk about what the things are that they're learning, so they can specifically tie in the subject matter that they're dealing with in school and their Christian worldview, and so that you can help them make those connections. Again, you don't have to know everything about that particular subject. You guys can work through that together. In fact, it's a great opportunity to have your students teach you about what they're learning. It's going to help them learn it, and then you can help them see the biblical worldview behind it.

paragraphs.heading: Private and public spheres
paragraphs.text: So what we often forget is that in the school world — and in a lot of our professional worlds too — we have this thing called two different aspects of our world. We have what's called the private sphere, and we have what's called the public sphere. This is important to get.

If you think of this as a house, this is your upstairs, where your bedrooms are, and what you think and what you do up in your bedrooms is your private business, right? Not many other people are going to be up there. But when you have people over for company or whatever, you have your public spheres. This would be your kitchen, your living room, those kinds of things. These are two different spheres of life, and the things that you do here are not the same as what you do here.

Oftentimes, the way we think is the exact same thing. So what our students — and sometimes we ourselves — will do is put our school or our jobs in our public life, and we'll talk about some things specifically there. But then we'll put our Jesus life up in our private sphere, and we separate these two things, and we don't want them to connect, and we learn to live that way. Just as I was taught in seventh grade, this is exactly what my teacher was telling me to do: separate these two things, live in a two-story home, and leave it that way.

paragraphs.heading: The bottom line
paragraphs.text: What we want to do is get rid of this and put Jesus down in our public space. So here's the bottom line. Science doesn't actually contradict our faith. Instead, it lays a crucial foundation for understanding our world.

paragraphs.heading: The bottle flip
paragraphs.text: Probably a year ago this became really popular, right — this little bottle flip thing, where you just flip a bottle and it's supposed to drop if you do it just right, like that. What's fascinating is that it seems like this is a huge thing of luck. I can just sit here and do this all day long, right? It's just this massive thing of luck, that I just happen to be getting lucky when I actually get the bottle to flip correctly. But the reality is that's not necessarily luck. Apparently it's not skill on the part of myself either. However, after a little bit of research, you find that this is actually more of a fine-tuning thing.

There's actually science behind the bottle flip. It has something to do with the size of the water bottle — this one being much too small — the amount of water that's in the bottle, and how much spin you actually put on it. If you get it right every single time, and you have just the right amount of spin, and just the right amount of water, and just the right bottle, you can never miss. Based on science, it'll always land the way it's supposed to. See?

paragraphs.heading: What if we had no Scripture
paragraphs.text: We learned from Genesis that this world was created by God. We know that, right? And we know that God designed it for us. But what if we really didn't have Scripture to tell us that? I mean, this tells me that God designed the world. This tells me that God did it all, and all I have to do is look at this and go, "Yeah, okay, I know that." But what if I didn't have it? What does this tell me about God's design? What it tells me is the same thing that nature tells us.

All of this fine-tuning, all of these things that we have — just right, just calculated just so, so that we could actually survive here, so that we could thrive, so we could live and breathe and do all the things that we do. And so we could have this earth spinning in this universe around the sun, in all the ways that most of us kind of just accept and take for granted and don't worry too much about. Is this really about random chance?

paragraphs.heading: Random chance or design
paragraphs.text: Did this world just sort of pop into existence, and things just happened to fall in the right way — that if I flip this bottle enough times, this universe just kept starting and restarting and restarting and restarting, until one day it actually worked? And see, there it is, now the universe worked. Is that what this is, or is this a well-crafted design by God?

That's what this unit is about, and that's what this lesson is about. This lesson is about looking at our universe and seeing that this is more than just a random whole bunch of stuff that happened to fall into place, the right place at the right time, but instead an actual design and science behind crafting the right conditions for life to happen. So for this week, I want you to think about one word. I want you to think about thinking.

paragraphs.heading: Science and faith together
paragraphs.text: Last week we kind of introduced the idea that science actually furthers our faith and lays a crucial foundation for what we believe. It's great.
