Well, this is where we start to see that happen. This is where we start to actually have to think about some of these things and start putting some pieces together. Think about more than just the thinking, cognitive piece of this and the stuff that you can know. But take a second and think through this for a second.

paragraphs.heading: A place made for us
paragraphs.text: What does it mean that God has made a place for us? If you stop and consider this for just one minute — all of these things, whether the atmosphere, the earth's rotation, the distance from the sun, whatever it is. These things are just so, so that we can live here, so that we can thrive here. If God designed this, it doesn't just prove or show evidence that God exists. It doesn't just prove that God gave us a place that's habitable, a place for us to actually just survive here.

But it's made in such a way that God has created a home for us. And he did it with his heart, and with love in mind. I mean, what does this say about who God is? What does fine-tuning say about the character of God?

paragraphs.heading: Halfway through the science unit
paragraphs.text: So here we are, about halfway through the science unit. I want to stop for a minute and get an idea of how you guys are doing. I want you to take a minute and think about a couple of things. One, how are your relationships doing? We've talked since the beginning about forming good relationships and creating a culture where questions are welcome, where students are being honest with you and with one another, and where their faith is developing. So take a step back, take some time this week, and analyze how that's going. Are your relationships furthering? Are they getting better? Are new students coming in? How are they assimilating? Those types of things.

paragraphs.heading: How students are tracking
paragraphs.text: The second thing is, how are students tracking? Now let's be honest: this is not easy. So ask yourself, and maybe even ask some of your students, how are they tracking? Is it all making sense, or do they just kind of nod their heads like they get it, but in the back of their minds they're going, I don't get it? Or are they super fired up, digging for more and asking great questions? Or are you everywhere in between? It's very possible. It could be all over the spectrum.

But take a second, stop, and think about where your students are, which leads to asking yourself: do I need to slow it down? Do I need to adapt things a little bit? Don't be afraid to pull back and revisit some concepts. Make sure there's understanding. Go back and ask some questions, and figure out and make sure that your students are exactly where you need them to be so that you can move forward successfully. Don't move forward until you are certain that your students are ready to do so.

paragraphs.heading: Two things to keep in mind
paragraphs.text: As you and your students are navigating some of these difficult waters, I want you to keep in mind two really important things. The first is the misconceptions that we've provided. These misconceptions are a clear window into the world of what your students are actually being taught. Now, they may not be taught these exact quotes or reading these exact things, but the stuff that we're quoting, the stuff that we're citing, is the underlying narrative that your students are reading about in textbooks in school.

paragraphs.heading: Examples that simplify
paragraphs.text: The second thing is the examples that you use. It's so important, if you can, to use the right kind of examples to simplify some of these difficult concepts and make them a little bit easier to understand. And the best example really is Sean's use of simply describing a book to help us understand DNA.

paragraphs.heading: Wrapping up science
paragraphs.text: So we've almost made it through science. We've discovered that science is really a foundation for understanding our world, and that it does not contradict our faith. Well, that's good news. We've also taken a look at three really good pieces of evidence that help us see that God is actually there — that we have evidence for God. We looked at the idea of fine-tuning, we looked at the idea of DNA, and we looked at the idea of design. All of these point to God in some way, shape, or form through the use of science.

paragraphs.heading: The eager student
paragraphs.text: Now, I want you to keep in mind two kinds of students this week. The first kind is the student who has all this information and is super fired up, ready to go with the best arguments they have to their teacher — who probably knows more than they do about all these things — especially this week with the idea of design, because this is where the conversation between creation and evolution starts to really come alive.

It might seem like this is a good idea for them to jump off and start all these arguments and try to win people to Christ. They might try it, and you want to champion that, but at the same time make sure that they do so in truth and love. If they're going to have these conversations, you don't want to tell them not to. It's okay that they can challenge their teachers, and it's okay to challenge their students, but to do so with love, and to do so with the appropriate amount of respect — especially for teachers — as well as engaging in the right kinds of conversations.

paragraphs.heading: The student still unsure
paragraphs.text: Now, the other type of student is maybe the one who really is still not sure, or the one who wasn't sure before entering into this conversation. Now would be a really good time to just take a step back and take inventory with that student, and ask them the plain question. Was this enough evidence? Do you need more? What further questions do you have? What clarifications do you need?

paragraphs.heading: Why we do this study
paragraphs.text: Now remember the reason why we're doing this study. It's so that our students can have a deep conviction for themselves about what they believe and why they believe it, and also be able to communicate that in love and humility, and do so relationally. So while it might be really exciting to have some eager students ready to get started and to get engaged in conversation, help them be patient, because there is so much more to learn.

paragraphs.heading: Morality is not simple
paragraphs.text: All right, so this week we're talking about morality. It might seem on the surface that talking about morality is pretty straightforward, right? It's right versus wrong. It's what we should be doing and what we shouldn't be doing, and we're really comparing all of that to God as the standard. So it seems pretty straightforward, pretty simple. But I want you to take a second and step back, because it may not be as simple as you think, or as you hope. I want you to think for a minute about what we're really asking students to do.

We're asking them to differentiate between right and wrong. And we're asking them to do that when they're taught that some of the things we're talking about are just a little bit more than mere opinion. Students are taught on a whole different level than maybe what we're used to, so you're going to experience something that maybe you don't realize you're going to experience. We stand on stage as leaders, and we're talking about Jesus, and we're talking about truth, and we're talking about these fundamental facts about the Christian faith, and we're telling them what they ought to be doing and what they ought not to be doing.

Students can often be looking at us while we're thinking we're talking about fact. We're thinking we're talking about pretty black-and-white kinds of things, and that may not necessarily be the case, when some of our students are looking up to us and thinking, "Well, that's your opinion. That's what you think, and I'm not sure I actually want to agree with your opinion."

paragraphs.heading: Meet with your small group leaders
paragraphs.text: So this is a good week. It's a good time to take a step back. Make sure you meet with your small group leaders, and make sure you talk through a little bit about what they might experience in their small groups. Talk a little bit about some feedback you can get from the students about some of the things you're talking about from the main stage: about what their thoughts are on right versus wrong, and what they're being taught in school, and how they feel about certain topics. You might be comforted, but you also might be surprised, and you might get some answers that you're not real thrilled with. But it's a good starting point, and something you can continue to work through.

paragraphs.heading: Copying homework in the hallway
paragraphs.text: I'll never forget, back when I was teaching, I'd walk in in the morning and you'd be stepping through the hallways. You had to literally step over all of the students who were sitting in the hallways and talking, all these great conversations and activity going on in the hallways. It was a great sort of experience in the morning, seeing some students' smiling faces and other students' not-so-smiling faces. It was awesome. And one day at a teacher's meeting, we got talking about some of the students, and we realized something that most of us were completely blind to: the students were doing more than just sitting in the hallways hanging out. The students were sitting in the hallways copying each other's homework for their first class, or their first couple of classes throughout the day.

Some of us talked about it: well, are they collaborating and working together on something, or are they just straight-up copying their homework, which would obviously be wrong? So we talked about it, we debated it a little bit, and then we decided, well, let's confront some of our students. Let's talk it through with some of our students. Maybe they just don't realize what they're doing, which would seem strange, but maybe they don't realize that what they're doing is wrong.

So we pulled a few students aside, with no intention of getting them in trouble, and just said, "Hey, what are you doing in the hallways in the morning?" And with no regard for possibly getting in trouble, or having us call their parents, or some kind of consequence coming down on them, they just said, "Yeah, we're just copying homework. That's what we're doing. No big deal." So we asked them, "Well, do you think this is wrong?" The response was simple: "Well, no." "Well, why not?" "Well, because we just don't." That was their answer. They just don't.

paragraphs.heading: Fact or opinion
paragraphs.text: And if you do a little bit of research into the world of education, and what students are being taught is right and wrong, it's actually becoming closer and closer to what we consider to be opinion. Students are being taught that any time we use words like "feeling," or what they believe, or what they think, it's simply an opinion. Well, this is sort of causing some problems, right? Because now we start talking about things well beyond copying homework as being an opinion.

When we say things like, well, are all men, or all people, created equally? Is that a fact, or is that an opinion? What about: it's wrong in our country to drink under the age of 21. Is that a fact, or is that just somebody's opinion? What about killing another unjustly? That's something we all consider, or at least hope we all consider, to be a universal truth: that killing another unjustly, as in murder, is wrong. Is that fact, or is that opinion? So the slippery slope that students are starting down is that these things are becoming a little bit more based on opinion. So then when we get into things like same-sex marriage: fact or opinion?

So as you stand on a main stage, or you stand in front of a group of students, and you start talking about what Scripture says is fact, they are being taught that these things are often just opinion. That is why talking about morality is vitally, vitally important in terms of helping them establish what our moral compass actually is and where we get our morals from.

paragraphs.heading: One Johnny tall
paragraphs.text: So here's a little story I like to tell when it comes to morality. It's a story about little Johnny. Little Johnny is a first or second grader who gets an assignment from school to go home and measure how tall he is. He fumbles around the house, trying to figure out how to measure himself, so that he can go back to school and be a huge success and get a great grade and all those wonderful things. He scrambles all over the house and can't figure out anything, and then finally he has this massively, beautifully wonderful idea.

He runs to school the next day, and all the little boys and girls are going up to the front of the class. Some say, "I'm this tall according to my dad," and "I'm this many basketballs high," and all these other different objects. Then Johnny gets up in front of the classroom, big smile, beaming, and says, "I'm one Johnny tall." The teacher kind of looks at him and reacts, and Johnny didn't pass the assignment, because we have no idea how tall Johnny really is. Johnny will never be more or less than one Johnny tall, no matter how big Johnny actually gets in the future.

We can't use ourselves to measure ourselves. We need something beyond us, something external to us, and morality functions the same way. And what's beautiful about morality, as much as it is difficult to follow what God desires for us to do, is that the fact that we have morals, the fact that we understand right from wrong, helps us see who God is. It points us to God. It gives us evidence for God, because we need something beyond ourselves to understand what the difference between right and wrong is.

paragraphs.heading: What you can do
paragraphs.text: So what can we do? There's a lot that's cautionary in all of that, so what can you actually do? Well, the first thing you can do is approach all of this first and foremost with grace and with love. Remember, most of your students, and I hope all of your students, really are just trying to love their friends and love people and be tolerant and get along and live peacefully among everybody else. I'm sure that's the case with almost all, if not all, of your students. So they're not trying to be malicious. They're not necessarily trying to defy authority. Approach them with a tremendous amount of grace and a tremendous amount of love, and listen. Listen to the reasons they're giving. That doesn't mean don't challenge those reasons, but make sure that you thoroughly, thoroughly listen to why they're saying what they're saying.

Secondly, know where they're coming from. Talk to them about where they're hearing their ideas: which classes, even which teachers. Is it at home? Is it online? Is it TV and media? Where are they getting these ideas from? Now, that doesn't mean you want to tell them, "All your ideas are stupid." You just want to hear where they're from, and hear again why they believe those things and why they think those things are true, and help them work through what those thoughts actually are. It's no different from helping you guys work through all of these topics, answering great questions and asking more great questions and trying to figure things out. You want to help students navigate this a little bit, rather than just shoot them down.

And finally, don't be afraid to challenge their thinking. Some students might come at you a little bit. Some students might get a little bit aggressive. Some might just shut down inside themselves if they feel like their opinion is not valued or not being heard. That's okay, as long as you draw that back out of them, and don't get offended if a student kind of comes at you. Challenge their thinking, but do so again in love and in understanding, and by listening and taking the time necessary.

And make sure that this is communicated to your small group leaders, because in that context, in that community, in the community that you are trying to build within your youth groups, it is so, so important that those students feel like they can open up, and that they feel like they can offer that opinion and be accepted, but also be challenged.

paragraphs.heading: Why beauty, agency and story
paragraphs.text: Last week we talked about morality, and the fact that morality points to God gives us some evidence that a divine Creator actually exists. Now, for these next couple of units, you might be thinking, "Well, why are we talking about beauty, agency and story?" These next few lessons are not as difficult as what we've tackled in the last couple of months, but don't gloss over them. Don't just fly through them like they're no big deal because they seem kind of strange. These are also incredibly important pointers to God, and they're going to help lay a foundation so that the students can see that God is present in their everyday lives, in the things they see and interact with on a daily basis.

paragraphs.heading: Where are your students?
paragraphs.text: So for this week, I want you to take a step back and do some evaluation. I want you to look at some of your students and take a minute to really try to figure out where some of them are. Ask yourself a number of questions. Do a little bit of evaluation to figure out how you're going to best move forward into this next half of your year. So the first thing I really want you to do is spend some time thinking about where your students are. Where are they?

And I don't mean that they're in youth group or they're not in youth group. I mean, where are they? If you paid attention at the very beginning, think about where they came in, what they were actually thinking about, and the questions that they had. Think about some of the questions they had, and some of the thoughts or beliefs they had. Those are all important for figuring out where they are now. You may have noted a few students specifically. I would go back and look at some of those notes and see whether there has been any change, good or bad. Do they have new questions? The questions they had — have those been answered?

paragraphs.heading: New students
paragraphs.text: Secondly, do you have any new students? Now that you've been going for a while, it's kind of easy to get into the rhythm and forget when new students arrive. This would be a great time to ask yourself: do you have some of our Essentials materials on hand? If I were you, I would always have five or six of our Essentials books on hand, ready to go any time a new student walks in the door, to make sure that they can be brought up to speed pretty quickly and that they don't feel super intimidated when they walk in the door and we're in the middle of this crazy big study that you guys are working on.

And if you have new students coming in, what are the questions that they have? Are they students who are seeking, or are they skeptics? Are they our traditional church students who just found a new church? Did they move? What's going on? Have some sort of matrix to understand where your students are coming from, so that as you move forward you can track this same question for these new students.

paragraphs.heading: Recurring questions
paragraphs.text: Are there recurring questions? Are there still questions? What I mean by this is, are they the same questions? Are you not answering questions? Do we have the answers yet? It's something to consider. Or are the students just constantly bringing up the same question? I don't mean questions about things you're going to get to, because you're going to get to those. I mean questions about anything that's within the curriculum so far. Are there recurring questions?

You might want to think about what you need to do — take some time, maybe pause, and actually answer these specific questions head on. Find the answers and get to them, so that the students can move on in their minds. A lot of times, if students get hung up on a question, they have a hard time moving through to the next thing. They need those things answered, and that's often true especially of some of your brighter students, who are super inquisitive and want to know things. If they have a question, they often have to have it answered. So you're going to want to stop and get those questions answered.

paragraphs.heading: Who is tracking, who pushes back
paragraphs.text: Which students are tracking? This is something we often forget about. Some of our students track really well, and it might be easy for you to get hung up on those students, because as you're talking to your group, or to the people in your small group, those are the ones who are talking a lot and raising their hand, or the students who are super engaged and really, really paying attention to you. It's easy to get focused on those students. It's good to notice it, but don't get overly focused on it, because what you're going to end up doing is forgetting that there are still students who are pushing back.

Are there students pushing back on you? Is there a student — and I don't mean verbally, I mean the kid in the back who's doing this, who has that look on their face that says, "I'm not buying it. I'm just not buying it." I would engage that student, not in front of everybody, but after it's all done — before, after, whenever there's a little more one-on-one time. Ask that student, "Hey, I noticed you seem kind of questioning. Do you have a question about what I was saying?" Don't be afraid to engage that student a little bit. Those are some of the most fun students.

But I'm going to put in a caveat, because there are probably a couple of different camps, depending on where you sit. Some of you are going to get focused here, because you want that affirmation — hey, everyone's listening to me, and this is great, and I've got these students tracking. To be honest, that's sort of my push: I love the students who really, really get engaged and ask great questions and those kinds of things. Some of you might get totally dialed in to what these students are doing, and you forget everybody else.

However, some of you might get really dialed in to these students instead — like, that's my project. I want to get that student. I want to do everything I can to make sure that student believes in Jesus before they walk out of here. I'm going to get that student to accept Jesus. That's a great goal, but don't do that and forget about everybody else. It's easy to get switched on to one or the other. There's everybody else in the middle, too, and you don't want to forget them either. But ask yourself where your students are, so you get a pretty good idea.

paragraphs.heading: A student I never forgot
paragraphs.text: I'll never forget one particular student that I had years ago in one of my apologetics classes. He sat in the back for probably the entire class, arms folded, feet up on the desk, looking at me like this is the dumbest class ever. Why am I here? I have to be here. I can't switch out of this class, and I'm stuck. I remember that every time I gave my lecture, or my talk, or the discussion — whatever we were doing for that day — I would focus it right on him, to make sure that I was talking to him. And I would look for little hints, little changes in the eyebrow or changes in posture and other nonverbals, just to see what he was thinking.

Then every day after class, as the students were walking out, I would ask, "So how was class today?" and ask further questions. What's going on? How are you? I'd see him in class, or in the hallway at different points in the day, and I would ask questions, even when he didn't say anything, just to get some nonverbals out of him, to see if I was making progress.

By the end, I never saw him accept Christ, but by the end he said, "There's something to what you're saying." That's all I ever got. I honestly don't know whatever happened after that. I just pray that somewhere along the line he has found Jesus. But at that moment, that was awesome, because I knew I was moving him in the right direction. Okay, so that's a whole lot of observations, a whole lot of stuff that you need to think through.

paragraphs.heading: How do you move forward?
paragraphs.text: So now you need to figure out: how do you move forward? How do you go to the next level? How do you do the next sort of things that we have coming? It might just be to keep going — keep on to the next thing, keep on doing the next thing, and it's no big deal. But it might be that you put the brakes on someplace. Do you go back to an old lesson and revisit something? Think it through, and don't be afraid to make some adjustments if that's what you need to do. Because remember, there are going to be ebbs and flows, and there are going to be ups and downs. But the goal is to provide our students with what they need to be prepared to move the gospel forward and to proclaim the kingdom. That's the goal.

paragraphs.heading: The ability to choose
paragraphs.text: The ability to choose. In fact, so many questions about why things happen are answered simply by humanity's ability to make a choice. Choices really are what govern so much of our lives, from the easiest decisions to some of the hardest, from choices that take forever to make to ones we make in an instant. Choices are so powerful. They are a privilege and they are a responsibility, and they are something that God has given us. This is one of those pointers, again, to who God is and to the fact that he exists.

But here's the key question. How do students' choices — how do all of our choices — actually reflect God? How do the things that we choose, whether they be right or wrong, good, bad, ugly, whatever it is, reflect God? Some of our choices obviously do. A lot of our choices obviously don't. But when we talk about our ability to choose, and about the fact that God gave it to us, there are some things we really have to make sure we nail down with our students.

paragraphs.heading: Two things to nail down
paragraphs.text: So we are challenging students with two things. Number one, that our free will points us to him. The fact that we have free will is a pointer to who he is. It helps us understand that because we have the ability to choose, God is out there somewhere. But number two, our free will should reflect him, and how we behave as Christians ought to be a reflection of who he is.

paragraphs.heading: Take your community's temperature
paragraphs.text: So as you go about your unit this week, I want you to keep something in mind. Last week we took the temperature of our students to figure out where the students are. This week I want you to take the temperature of your community. We talked at the very beginning about the importance of establishing a community — a strong community, a community that is open, one that loves, one that's close, one that students feel safe in. We talked about that as kind of an overarching goal: that being able to communicate truth and love means having a community where students feel safe to ask questions and so forth.

So how is that community doing? How is it working? Are there adjustments that you need to make? It's so easy, especially as a leader of large groups, to try to figure out how all of these groups are working. Are there other issues, or are there not? Does everybody feel that they belong? Even if you only do a small group yourself, it's really easy to get caught up and forget about maybe one particular student who has a ton of really great things to say, but who for some reason doesn't feel like they can say those things. So it's good to take a step back, take a look at our communities, and see whether we are hitting the mark, where we want to be.

paragraphs.heading: Four questions for leaders
paragraphs.text: So here are a couple of things I want you to think about. Are leaders providing the right atmosphere? Are they crafting that sort of atmosphere of discussion — one where questions are welcome, one of grace and love but with truth, not letting one student dominate, inviting all students to participate? All of those pieces of the puzzle: is the right kind of atmosphere being fostered?

Number two, are students being loved? And are they being challenged? So often we kind of confuse the two, and we think that we are loving students when really we are just letting them think what they want to think. In my experience, the most challenged students that I had — in terms of how much I challenged them — were the ones who felt most loved at the end of a year. Those are the ones who felt like they were valued.

Go to any school, in any classroom, where in the middle of things students are frustrated, they're under pressure, and they think a teacher or somebody is really too hard on them, and they complain about it. If you notice, go back to those schools and ask those teachers how many graduates come back to see them. The number is probably pretty high. It sort of works this way: the more challenging you are with a student, the greater the respect you gain and the greater the love that you are showing them. It just works that way. So make sure that you love them, but make sure that you also challenge them.

Number three, do they feel safe to be honest? I mean, if we're loving them properly, then that's probably going to be the case, that they do feel safe. But there are some things we want students to be honest about, and sometimes their honesty causes us to have to react in a way that they don't want us to react. But do they feel safe? Do they feel like they can be honest with us and that we are going to react appropriately?

Number four, are your small groups serving one another? Are you, in your small groups, caring for one another? Have you created a community where you love each other, or where the students are loving on each other? It isn't just a place where you kind of come together, say a few things, and then off you go into something else and off to your real friends, or whatever the case is. Are your small groups becoming a tight-knit community of people who care and love for one another? I would encourage you, as a next step for that, to take those students and get them out into the community — whether it be the wider community or even just the church community — and find places for them to serve together and do things together to help build and foster that kind of community.

paragraphs.heading: Almost at the halfway point
paragraphs.text: All right, so you've almost made it to the halfway point. Congratulations, keep it up. You guys are doing a great job, I am sure. And remember, some of your students might be starting to feel some of the stress of school, because you're probably getting around midterms and finals and tests and quizzes and those kinds of things. So now would be a really good time, and this is a really good lesson, to do some fun things, to have some fun with students on making choices — whether it be through games, whether it be through examples, something silly, where you could have a whole bunch of fun having students make choices but at the same time teach them the power of those choices.

paragraphs.heading: Story comes from God
paragraphs.text: We all love a great story, so this lesson should be a fun one. But I want you to remember that students need to see that story originates from God himself. Again, this is another pointer to God, showing students that God exists because we have these things — because we have such a thing as story, because we can tell great stories. And as people who reflect the image of God, we get that from him. It's awesome, and hopefully your students will see that at the end of this unit.

paragraphs.heading: Finding redemptive themes
paragraphs.text: A fun way to do this is to find different stories, whether it be your own story, or maybe some of their stories, or the story of someone you know. It could be a book; it could be a movie. But within those stories you want to find redemptive themes, themes of salvation, those kinds of things. And you'd be surprised how many different stories are actually based off of, or have buried within them, biblical themes.

paragraphs.heading: Your midterm
paragraphs.text: So now you are officially halfway through the curriculum. You've had some time to take inventory of where you are — where you are with your students, with your leaders, with your small groups and the community, and those types of things. You've had a chance to step back, take a look at all of that, and see how the year is going so far. Now it's time to evaluate. This might not be something you're used to doing, but I highly encourage it. I think it's really, really helpful in moving forward. So we're going to call this your midterm. Get ready, because you have a quiz and a test coming up and you're going to need — no, I'm just kidding. I just have two suggestions, and it's super simple.

paragraphs.heading: Have students teach it back
paragraphs.text: The first thing is something I've been doing for years with students that I think is awesome: have them do something. Instead of just having them listen and maybe engage in discussion, have some students — you might pick out one, you might pick out several — choose one of their favorite lessons, a favorite topic or a part of a lesson, and either teach it back, lead a discussion, or do something with it. That's fun. It doesn't mean they have to be crazy or super complicated, but it helps you and helps your leaders get an idea of whether your students are digesting this and are able to communicate it back.

If they can accurately communicate something back to you, they've got it. It's a simple, easy way to determine whether or not they're tracking with you. You can ask them all day long and they might say yes, but when they try to say it, they're all over the place and they don't get it. But if they can teach it back, it will compel other students, and it changes things up. It's kind of fun, it's something different, and they can have some fun with it. This is a really good time to do that, now that you are halfway through.

paragraphs.heading: Where you got stuck
paragraphs.text: The second thing is to take a look at where you struggled. You don't want to keep moving forward if for some reason you got stuck on something. So now might be a good time to think about how to unstick yourself from that particular topic. Maybe there's something you just weren't comfortable with, or something they didn't get, or a place where you want some reinforcements. Maybe there were some additional questions that you just couldn't answer. Maybe it's simply a matter of you sitting down, doing some more research, and figuring it out — that would be awesome. Maybe it's an additional video you find someplace else, or maybe it's bringing in the experts, bringing in somebody.

On our website at AwanaYM.org, we are going to have for you a list of potential people that you can get a hold of. I can't guarantee they're going to come, but you can get a hold of them to see if you can schedule a time to bring in one of many apologetics experts to help you, or to do a special event, or to do something to further the sticky point or just further a discussion that was already started.

paragraphs.heading: Great job so far
paragraphs.text: So great job getting this first half of the year completed. I know these first few months probably have been difficult. There have been some topics you had to tackle that maybe you've been a little less than comfortable with, and some things that maybe have been challenging for you and your students. But I know you have done a phenomenal job of getting the information to the students, engaging with them at a high level, making this stuff super relevant, and stressing its importance as they continue their walk with Christ.

And if you're struggling anywhere, for any reason, on anything, please reach out to us. We are here to help you. You can email us, and you can hit us up on Twitter or Facebook. We have a series of videos called In Two Minutes that we designed specifically for students, and in the comments below those we invite students to ask additional questions. Through those questions, we will continue to add additional videos and answer additional questions. Again, we are here to help you. Please reach out to us, and we will help you in any way that we can.

paragraphs.heading: Miracles point to God
paragraphs.text: So it's Unit 5, Lesson 1, and we get to talk about miracles. As you start to prepare for this week, I don't want you necessarily just thinking, "I've got to prove to my students that miracles exist." We're going to show a little bit of that, but more so that because there are miracles, it points to the fact that God exists. We start off — if you just look at what the students are going to study in their Bible — we actually chose 1 Kings 18 for that very reason.

When you look at that particular miracle, the miracle of Elijah and the prophets of Baal, and a huge fire came down and ignited the sacrifice, and how that represented God's sovereign power — that miracle is just another way we can see it. Among all the things that Jesus did, all the things in the Bible, this is a really, really cool example of how God showed up and performed a miracle so that we can see exactly who God is.

paragraphs.heading: The intro experience
paragraphs.text: As students begin this week and start reading, the intro experience is going to walk them through what to think about when it comes to miracles and what that looks like. We ask them specifically: what's the most improbable event in human history? Just have them think through, what would be an improbable event? Things like this: it's not likely that if I stepped outside right now I'd get struck by lightning. That's probably not going to happen. If I walked outside and a meteor just crashed on earth and annihilated me and everybody around — probably not going to happen, but it is an improbable event, the same as a miracle.

So the intro experience for the students is really to get them thinking through: when we talk about a miracle, what are we talking about? You might get some answers when you start talking with your students. You might actually get things like, "Is it a miracle that when you're out shopping during the Christmas season, a parking spot right by the door opened up? Is that a miracle and a sign from God that you got that parking space?" Probably not. Is that a miracle? Is it a miracle when a child is born? We call it the miracle of birth, but is that really a miracle? We're talking about miracles that we see in Scripture. That's where you want your students to start to think through and get an idea of what exactly we're talking about when we're talking about a miracle.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing your storyteller
paragraphs.text: So let's talk for a second about your storyteller. It might have been difficult up to this point, and it may be difficult moving forward, to find the perfect person for your storyteller. You might have had to search high and low, and maybe this is one of those spots where you're thinking, "I really don't know exactly who I want for a storyteller." For this week, I might suggest you use a student. Find a student who maybe has witnessed a miracle — maybe a miraculous healing.

I once had a student whose story was hard to refute, because she was such a trusted and honest student. We knew that she was telling the truth and that her experience was real. She was on a missions trip in Africa, and she was praying over a young girl, and this young girl's legs were not the same somehow. She can't explain it, and she would tell you today that she has no idea what exactly happened or how it happened.

But she knew some kind of miracle happened. As they were praying, it felt to her like this little girl's leg grew enough that they were the same. She told me, "Mr. Kozak, I don't know if this is real. I don't know if this is true, but I feel like this happened." She felt like she was a witness to an actual miracle, a little bit like what goes on in Scripture. None of us were there, and none of us can verify it, but it was a really fascinating story that helped students see the power of a miracle.

What she thought happened, what she saw happen, deeply impacted her. Today she still regularly goes to Africa and serves as a missionary there on and off, as much as she possibly can. That moment deeply impacted her, and I'm sure it impacted a lot of her fellow students. So this is one of those times when it might be really cool to find a student — maybe not with that crazy of a story, but a story nonetheless — a student who has witnessed a really divine, real miracle.

paragraphs.heading: Large group time
paragraphs.text: As you get ready to engage students in large group time, I want you to keep one thing in mind. The misconception we've given you — that science can explain away miracles — is a very real reality in the life of our students. They're taught that, and they're conditioned to believe it. They're conditioned for that to be the default. Instead of thinking right away that something might be a miracle, they're conditioned to think right away that something can just be explained by science.

There should be a healthy balance, because there are a lot of things we might think are miracles that end up being able to be explained. But there are also a lot of things we think we can explain that really end up actually being a miracle. We really can't explain it as well as we think, and science doesn't provide that kind of explanation. Science can't explain the supernatural. So be aware, as you're preparing your lesson, and figure out: how do I communicate to students that miracles can actually happen, and the difference between what science can explain and what science cannot explain? That's going to compel students to start to think about whether miracles can really happen today, and maybe more importantly, whether miracles can happen right here and right now.

If you think about it, you're probably going to get some questions. This may happen more in your small group time, but you're going to get some questions. I can almost guarantee that students will start asking, well, if miracles can happen, how come I don't see miracles happening in my space, in my culture, in my sphere of influence, in my family and those kinds of spaces, in the same way that we saw miracles in Scripture?

If you just look at the very early stages of Acts, Peter and John walk up to the temple. There's a lame man in front of the temple. He can't walk; he's never been able to walk. The Bible tells the story of Peter simply reaching his hand out and saying, "I don't have any money, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus, get up and walk." And the guy gets up and walks, and he's instantaneously healed. What's fascinating about that story is that this man had never been able to walk since birth — complete muscle atrophy in his legs — and all of a sudden his ankles become strong. He's jumping up and down. He's walking.

So students are going to ask the question: how come those miracles don't happen here today? Well, they might not happen in your city all that frequently, if ever. They might not happen in this country all that often or that frequently. But we don't know that they don't happen. They might, and it's likely that they do happen — maybe not to that degree, I don't know. But we can't discount it. We can't say they just don't happen. They might happen, and God has the power to make that happen if He so chooses. So miracles of a biblical proportion, I would argue, are still possible.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: While students are in small groups, encourage your small group leaders to really take time this week to ask — maybe to pry a little bit — to see whether your students are really convinced. Convinced of a couple of things. First, are they convinced that miracles are even possible at all, that it's even a possibility? Take note of that. Have your small group leaders actually take note of that, because it's going to become important next week when we start talking about the resurrection of Jesus. Are your students convinced that miracles are at least possible?

Number two: are your students convinced that miracles have happened in their midst — whether by their friends, or by people they know, or things they have read? Are they convinced that miracles have actually happened? Yes, first they have to be convinced that miracles are possible in order to be convinced that they have happened. Walk them through that process, and then, if they're not convinced, ask them what it would take.

What would it take to help them see the probability and the possibility of miracles all around them? Do they have to open up their view of God? Do they have to open up their view of who Jesus is and what the cross is all about? We'll get to that next week. What has to happen for them, do they think, in order to make miracles a reality in their mind, so that they can even see some of the things that God is up to?

paragraphs.heading: When miracles get personal
paragraphs.text: One thing to keep in mind as you're navigating through this: although we talk a lot about the fact that miracles are possible and verifiable and that they do happen, and we see throughout Scripture that God works in mighty ways, and we want to boast that miracles happen all throughout the world, this can also be a very, very personal thing. Miracles can bring up really, really important questions in the lives of our students.

How come God performed a miracle in this person's life, but not in my life? How come God healed this person, but not this person? It almost feels like God is picking and choosing. How does that work, and how do you walk with students through difficult times like that? I'm going to be honest with you: there's really not a specific answer that I can give you — a "Well, God does this because…" It's not there. But your job as a leader is to walk alongside your students and help them in their specific situations, to navigate those particular circumstances in those particular parts of their lives, so that they grow closer to Christ and not further away.

paragraphs.heading: A conversation with students
paragraphs.text: Several years ago I was talking to a group of students, and I was explaining to them basically what's in 1 Corinthians 15. I was explaining the fact that without the resurrection, Christianity would cease to exist. It was once described to me that it's almost as if the resurrection were a tiny little thread connected to the fate of the world, and if we were to cut that thread, everything would fall apart. I was explaining this to my students, and the looks on their faces were priceless. You could tell that they didn't know anything I was explaining to them. It was all new news to them. They knew the resurrection. They were good Christian kids. They knew and believed that Jesus had resurrected, and they knew that it had something to do — or maybe everything to do — with their salvation.

But they hadn't realized: what if Jesus hadn't resurrected? What if he had just stayed in the grave? We always talked about how Jesus was crucified for our sins, but he was also resurrected. So there's that second piece in the equation that's really super important. Then I said to them, did you know that there's historical evidence behind the resurrection? Well, that was a whole other look on their faces that I can't even describe. It was fascinating, but it was so encouraging to me, because I knew that there was something to be taught here, and that there was something these students were going to gain from what I was telling them.

paragraphs.heading: Jesus as a historical figure
paragraphs.text: It's likely that you're going to get some of those same looks as you start to talk with some of your students about this, because so many students know that Jesus existed. I mean, let's face it — it's not a new thing that Jesus was a historical figure. You're going to get a few people on the fringe who believe otherwise, but all mainline history says Jesus existed. He was crucified by the Romans. He was buried in a tomb. And what? It's reported that he rose three days after. Interesting.

But there's history behind it, which is why we focus on Paul's comments in 1 Corinthians 15, to help students start to see the importance of the resurrection before we dive into the historical reliability of the resurrection. We want them to really get the whole picture of it, along with the fact that even in chapter 15 Paul gives a little bit of that historical account. Jesus appeared to people. He appeared to the twelve, and he appeared to more than 500 people. The way Paul says this is almost as if he's saying, "Hey, they're alive. Go check it out. Go ask them. If you don't believe me, it's no big deal."

So as your students are going through their intro experience, we want them to start to think about a historically documented and verified event that happened before their lifetime. We want them to go into history, and a good place to do this is really in their history books. How much of the Roman Empire do we know about? How much of Alexander the Great do we know about? How much of the Civil War do we know about? How much of the historical events that happened long before us do we actually have information on?

We want them to start to see it, because as much as we look at Scripture — because it is the Word of God, and it's wholly inspired, and it's awesome — we can also take a step back and say, well, what does this say from a historical perspective? What does it say about Jesus as a historical person? What does it say about the resurrection as a historical event? We want students to start thinking of the resurrection, just for a moment, as a historical event. That's what this exercise is really designed to do: to connect them to the idea that the resurrection is actually history.

paragraphs.heading: Finding a storyteller
paragraphs.text: Okay, so for your storyteller, I would recommend going to a local college or a local Christian high school and finding somebody who is a history professor or a history buff, or somebody who really knows not just history, but how to tell history well. Find someone who knows how to tell the story of history. I say that because that's really what the Gospels are doing. The Gospels are the account of Jesus. We know this, but it's a story that's describing history.

So if you can get someone who can do the same thing with another piece of history, you'll be able to help students start to make that connection and start to see the Gospels as this historical narrative that wells up and culminates with the death and resurrection of Christ. It's a very cool picture. If you do it right, you can paint it really, really well.

paragraphs.heading: Answering the myth
paragraphs.text: We want to make sure of something. It's not a huge issue among students, but it is out there, and they will run into it when they get to college: the claim that the resurrection was just a myth. So, yeah, okay, Jesus died, and it's a myth that the church made up that he resurrected. It's important that we help students see that that's not historically accurate. We'll get into more of why that is as we move forward over the next couple of weeks, but it's important to help students see that this is something they're going to hear as they go into college and beyond.

Okay, so students are going to be able to see at the end of this that the resurrection is actually historical. Now, does that mean that we can say this is a for-sure thing and that it's absolute? Well, I would say, yeah, of course it is, but that's a bit different. Can we prove that Jesus resurrected? Well, not beyond a shadow of a doubt, of course not. But we can't do that with anything in history, right? We can't prove too many things in history beyond a shadow of a doubt, because we weren't there.

But the way history is done — and what you'll see even from the storyteller, the historian — is that the one with the best evidence is the one who gets to say what happened. So the question is: do we have the best possible evidence for the resurrection? There are a couple of things that I want to make sure you can explore more deeply. You can get into a little bit more. You can present it to your students. You can get into discussions about this within your small group time. If your students want to go a little bit deeper, there are some really cool things you can do.

paragraphs.heading: The resurrection as history
paragraphs.text: So, the resurrection as history. Now, when we think of history, most people think of, well, it's the Bible, right? So the number one place we all look is the Bible. The Bible could be viewed as a history book. That's the Word of God. We don't want to make it a textbook, but there's history in it. Okay, that's great. So there's some evidence there. We have one piece of evidence in the Bible. But what do people say? Well, that's the Bible, and you can't believe everything the Bible says. We'll get into that later. Actually, we can — but we'll get into that later.

But what else, then? Are there other things? What about outside of the Bible? Are there things outside of the Bible that give us clues that Jesus resurrected? There are. There are Jewish historians. There are Roman historians who recorded events about the resurrection — that at least the disciples of the early years thought that Jesus resurrected, and who recorded that they were reporting that Jesus resurrected. So that's important. There are early Christian writings like the Didache, and letters from a church father named Clement, that talk about the resurrection. These aren't in the Bible. They're good Christian writings, the stuff that we still use and study in the world of scholarship to figure out what's going on historically. But that's awesome. And you've got even now skeptics, people who aren't Christians, saying that Jesus was reported as resurrected.

Now, this kind of raises the question. All right — if all of these areas say that Jesus resurrected, or at least give us clues to know that people believed that he did, that's pretty good. Well, maybe there are other explanations. Maybe there are other things going on. Every other explanation given has to provide more evidence, better evidence, than the hypothesis, if you will, that he resurrected. And when you do that, without going into all the details, they all fall short. There's the one that says he just sort of fainted, that he wasn't really dead, so therefore he didn't have to worry about it. There are ones that say he wasn't actually buried in the tomb, that he was buried in a shallow grave and some birds and wild dogs ended up eating his body.

There are some people who say they just grabbed a body and pretended it was Jesus, and it really wasn't. There are all kinds of different theories, none of which have the same amount of evidence as the resurrection. So this is exactly why we wanted to connect it with history. When we look at other historical events and how much evidence there is for those, we have just as much or more for the resurrection as for pretty much most other historical events, especially historical events that happened around the same time. And we'll see that when we talk about Scripture specifically. So help your students see that this was a historical event, and that there's evidence for it as a historical event.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: But just like last week, I would do the same thing that you did last week. I'd go into your small groups and I would ask them, number one: are you convinced that it's at least possible that the evidence points to Jesus resurrecting? And number two: if you are convinced, what does that mean? We talked in the very beginning about the importance of the resurrection, right? If the resurrection is out there, all of Christianity falls down. So if you're convinced of the resurrection, what does that now mean for your life? What needs to change? What needs to be furthered? How does your spiritual walk need to go even further than maybe it is now? What does that mean for you? What does that mean for how you talk to other people about the resurrection and Jesus and who he is, and what the crucifixion and resurrection actually mean, and what salvation is all about?

Ask students not just whether they believe this stuff, but have them dig into, okay, now what? What does all this mean? What do I do with all this information? And if they're not convinced, and they're still kind of going, "I'm not sure," that's okay. But now is the time when you can start digging a little bit into, okay, well, what questions do you continue to have? What roadblocks are there that I can help knock down? What do I need to do to help bring you along a little bit, or better, to help you understand these things a little bit more deeply? Is it a misunderstanding? Is it that I'm just not getting something? Or is it something bigger?

Now is the time that you might start to see some roadblocks in some students' lives, some walls they might put up. They might want to believe this stuff. They might really love the idea, but they might still hold back. And as you walk alongside these students, you're going to need to start figuring out why that is and what's going on. That's why we talked at the very beginning about the importance of building relationships, because now it's going to start to really matter. If it hasn't mattered before, now it's really going to get there, because there are going to be some major changes going on in your students' lives.

paragraphs.heading: Do they believe Jesus is God?
paragraphs.text: When you're talking to your students about Jesus, do you automatically assume that they believe Jesus to be God? For years I did. I just assumed it, until I got into a conversation with them about it and realized that that's not always the case. Not that long ago, I was talking with a couple of young guys who came to my door. They were Mormons.

They were super nice and very friendly, and I had a great conversation with them. Naturally I went right to talking about Jesus, because at first we agreed on a ton of things, which I expected to be the case. But then, once we started talking about Jesus, although it seemed like we were going to agree, I very quickly realized that where I thought we would disagree is exactly where I thought we would disagree. And I went right to John 8. What I love about this passage is that Jesus just flat out says it. He says who he is, which is partly why — almost entirely why — the Pharisees and the religious leaders want to kill him, because Jesus says, "Before Abraham was born, I am."

And I asked these guys, what do you think Jesus means here? What do you think this is? They stumbled over it, and they really couldn't come up with a good answer, so they flipped to another passage and started talking about something different. I tried to redirect them back, and it reminded me of a lot of the conversations that I've had with students over the years — and of me making that mistake of just assuming that when we talk about Jesus, we're talking about the same thing.

paragraphs.heading: Who Jesus claims to be
paragraphs.text: So it's very possible that even in your context, when you talk about Jesus, you may be talking on a different plane than some of your students are. But this is a great opportunity to be crystal clear on exactly who it is that Jesus actually is, and who he says he is. That's why we have students focus right in on John 8, because it's here that Jesus makes the flat-out statement, "Before Abraham was born, I am." The focus here is who Jesus claims to be.

paragraphs.heading: The intro activity
paragraphs.text: So we ask students in the intro activity to put down who they think they are, what their family and friends would say about them, and then whether that matches up. And do they have evidence for this? They think they're somebody — they think they're a soccer player, or a Christian, or a musician, or a football player, or whatever. Do they have evidence for it? I used to call myself a football player because I played football, but a person once brought it up to me and said, "You don't really play football." I said, "Well, what do you mean?" He said, "Well, you sit the bench." So was I really a football player? Probably not so much. So who do they think they are, and what evidence do they have for it?

So the trick of it is that if Jesus says who he is, and we have evidence for who he says he is, now we've got something. If someone says they're a basketball player and they scored 35 points the night before, they're clearly a basketball player. There's evidence for it. So this is the time you can actually have your students do some of this interaction — nicely and gently and with respect, of course — with each other in your large group time, to get at this idea of: do I have evidence for who I think I am? And do I have evidence for who somebody else thinks that they are? So it would be a good opportunity to do some of that interaction.

paragraphs.heading: Just a good moral teacher
paragraphs.text: In your small group time, one thing that I bet is probably going to come out — and you'll want to make sure your small group leaders are ready to deal with it — is this: it's not hard, I don't think, to look at Jesus as a great moral teacher, as someone who has this wonderful religious sage kind of vibe going on, where they can read what he says about love and forgiveness and acceptance and mercy and justice and all these great things that Jesus talks about, like in the Sermon on the Mount, and leave it there.

And then go on and say, "I'm going to try to follow what Jesus says as a good moral teacher, but I'm not ready to accept him as the God of the universe, the creator of all — because if I accept him as the God of the universe and the creator of all, that has wider implications for me than I'm ready to accept."

See, it's easy to accept him as a good moral teacher, because I can choose to ignore his teachings if I so choose to. I can do whatever I want when I want. And when I choose to follow his teachings, I look awesome. If I don't, no one's really going to notice. But if I'm held accountable to the God of the universe, that's a whole other story.

paragraphs.heading: What I saw in my students
paragraphs.text: So believe it or not, one thing that I found among some of my students back when I was teaching was that a lot of students really loved Jesus and really liked what he taught, but had very little to no intention of ever following him as God. And that bothered me. It was right there. It was under my nose, and half the time I don't even know if I noticed it. But after a while it became very apparent, once I started looking for it. So it changed the way I taught, and it changed the way I started to converse with some of my students, and I started to challenge them.

paragraphs.heading: Who do you say I am?
paragraphs.text: And I think small group, in this time and in this lesson, might be a perfect opportunity for you to challenge your students with this question: how do you see Jesus? It's similar to how Jesus addressed Peter in Matthew chapter 16 — "Who do you say I am?" Ask your students, who do you say Jesus is? And when they answer you, whatever their answer is, ask them why. Get some answers out of them as to why they think that.

And if they're in that place where Jesus is just a good moral teacher, ask them what it would take to get them to see him as God. Is there enough evidence? I mean, you've presented the evidence, and there's a whole bunch of it. If you look through all the verses, we've only given you a spattering of the verses that show that Jesus is God. So what does that mean for them? Is there not enough evidence, or are they just not willing? It can be an eye-opening experience.

I'll be honest: I'm not telling you if there's anything you can actually do about it physically right at this moment. But it definitely will change the way you approach those students, the way you address them, the way you teach them, the way you pray for them. So I would encourage you to dive into that. It's sort of a scary place to dive into, a little bit, but I would encourage you to do that.

paragraphs.heading: Coming down from the mountaintop
paragraphs.text: If you've been leading youth for any time, you've probably done a retreat. And if you've been leading youth for any time and you've done a retreat, then you've probably had that mountaintop experience where students you didn't at all expect would meet Jesus in that space did. It was awesome, and you loved every minute of it, right? And then you come down from the mountain, so to speak. Then Monday comes, and all of a sudden it starts to feel like we're right back to where we were.

I think a lot of that is because it's super cool to love Jesus when we're at camp and everybody around us loves Jesus. It's super cool to talk about discipleship and spiritual formation, and talking about Jesus to the lost, and going out and being a witness for Christ in a world that desperately needs to hear the gospel. All of that is super cool to talk about, and it's exciting when we're in this little pressure cooker of Christians.

And so often we go out, and we send our students out, and they come back the same way they were, and we're left saying, what the heck happened? It's because Christianity is not super cool out there. It may be super cool in your youth group — which is awesome — but it's not necessarily super cool out there. It's easy to be a Christian inside the context of a youth group, right? It's easy to be a Christian when we're up at camp. It's easy to be a Christian around other Christians. What happens when we need to be a follower of Jesus around everyone else? Not so easy.

paragraphs.heading: The lives of the apostles
paragraphs.text: One thing your students are going to get a chance to learn this week is about the lives of the apostles. Now, we don't know a whole lot about the lives of the apostles, but what we do know is that many of them gave, and all of them were willing to give, their lives for the message that they preached. I love what Peter and John say in Acts 4:20, that we can do nothing but speak of the things that we have seen and heard. Even in the face of persecution, where they're being told, don't speak about Jesus anymore, because if you do there are going to be serious consequences. Guess what? They said, no, we're not going to do it. I'm still going to talk about Jesus. You can't stop us, and there's nothing you can do to us to stop us. That's awesome.

Several times I've prayed, man, God, can I just have that kind of boldness? And yes, I've done the whole thing with my students where I've asked them, if someone held a gun to your head and told you to denounce Jesus, would you? That may be becoming more of a reality in our world now more than ever. But the bottom line is that we want our students to see the power of the Holy Spirit in our lives and the power of the gospel, and how it ought to compel us to move into spaces where the gospel needs us most, despite the fear, despite the difficulty. That really becomes the focus this week as you get into some things.

We want students to know that the apostles were not liars — that despite what some people say, they didn't make this stuff up. Why would you give your life over for something you know is completely a lie? That doesn't quite work. And they were willing to die for this belief. That's a profound reality for our students to get after, and it should be a very transformative experience for them.

paragraphs.heading: Others die for their beliefs
paragraphs.text: I know what many students are probably going to say to you, and you're probably going to hear this: others have died for their belief. Especially in our world, we hear about it all the time, especially with terrorism — others die for their belief. What makes the apostles so much different, right? They're fervent too. They think what they believe is right. So how come the apostles are different? Yes, that's absolutely true. But here's the difference, and this is something you're going to hear Sean say; I'm just going to echo it. If I died for my faith and I proclaimed it to be true, that's just because I think it's true. It doesn't necessarily make it true. It's because it's been passed down to me, and I think I've got it all figured out, I think I've got it all right, and I'm going to believe that I do.

paragraphs.heading: Eyewitnesses, not just believers
paragraphs.text: But the difference is that the apostles saw and were eyewitnesses to Jesus. That's why they're apostles: they actually lived with Jesus, walked with Jesus, saw him die, saw him resurrect, were given the instructions, and they died as a result of that belief. It's a direct correlation, right?

So you've got this piece to it: here is Jesus, this counter-cultural public figure, an icon, a religious type of person who is spreading news that is totally contrary to what the mainline beliefs were, whether you were Jewish or Roman. So there was fear, there was animosity, there was, who is this guy? What is he doing? What's going on? Then once he was gone, it was like, whew, he's out, we're done. Let's move on.

And then all of a sudden these apostles, these people who were with Jesus, start carrying this on. Now imagine for a moment that this is not true, and you're one of the apostles, and you get told: shut it down, or you're going to lose your life. What do you pick? I'm not going to carry this lie. There's nothing in it for me. What do I care? You're not going to die for something you know is a lie. But they so believed it — the resurrection changed them so much — that they were willing to have their lives put to an end, in some horrific ways, mind you. Now, it doesn't prove anything beyond the shadow of a doubt, but it does show that the apostles were not lying.

paragraphs.heading: Small group discussion questions
paragraphs.text: So in your small group time, focus in on the student discussion questions. Specifically: how would you describe the conviction the apostles had for their message? Dive into that a little bit deeper. How would you describe their conviction? And do you agree with their conviction? Ask your students honestly: did these apostles seem absolutely out of their minds? Why would you do this? Or is there something more going on here?

Help them make the connection of what it would be like if you were there. Try to connect them to it and bridge the gap between then and now, and bring your students into that space now. Find an example, find something that will help them understand: if you absolutely saw something and you knew it to be true, how far would you go to make sure that truth came out? How far would you go? We see it all the time in movies and media and music and other places, where we want the truth to come out and we're willing to go to great lengths to make sure of that. So how far would they go?

The third one is, what fate did the apostles meet due to their relentless devotion to spreading the gospel? Have them look back into that. Now, there is some wide disagreement on the exact fate of some of them, and you can look into that. Be careful what you find if you go looking on the internet. Not all of it is 100% accurate. There are some things that are church tradition, not necessarily historically accurate, but it still makes the point that they did suffer and die as a result. How they suffered and died is a little bit up for debate, but we know that they did, for sure.

And lastly, what does the apostles' fate mean for the faith of your students? This is going to get into the nitty-gritty of things, because this seems so distant, right? This seems so far off, something so old that it doesn't really matter anymore. It doesn't concern me. I'm in my nice, comfy whatever. It's fine. Bring it. What does it mean for them? Have them think that through and talk it through specifically. Make them dig deep. If they give an answer that leaves you asking, why? — ask them to go a little bit deeper and really pull out of them what it would mean. And what does it now mean moving forward? How are they going to live differently? How are they going to act differently, knowing this information?

paragraphs.heading: Looking back over the unit
paragraphs.text: Then take some time and look back at what you've looked at over the last couple of weeks. You've got miracles. A miracle is verifiable. It's testable. We know that miracles exist. We see the greatest miracle in the history of the world in the resurrection of Jesus. That resurrection miracle solidifies the claim that Jesus is God, the Creator of all. And that message of the gospel, and who Jesus is, and what was going on in the world, was so compelling, so powerful, so life-changing that the apostles who saw it, witnessed it and lived it died because of it. That's powerful, powerful testimony.

Have your students look back on the whole blanket of concepts that we've just laid out over the last four weeks. Have them take a hard look at their faith and say, now how do I move with all this knowledge? I can't stay here. I can't just know this and move on. Now that I know all of this, what does it look like for me moving forward in my walk with Christ?

paragraphs.heading: An allegedly biblical document
paragraphs.text: Just this morning I was reading an article about a biblical document — or an allegedly biblical document — that was about 1500 to 2000 years old. This document is called the Epistle of Barnabas. The article said that this epistle claimed that Jesus never actually resurrected. In fact, it said that Jesus was simply a prophet, that Jesus ascended to heaven without dying, and that Judas Iscariot was actually crucified in Jesus's place.

Now, if you've ever read this book, then you know that none of those things are in it the way I've just described them. But here is an article that says this is true, that this is astounding new information we have about Jesus. As Christians, though, we know that this book, the Bible, is what tells us the truth of Christianity. Which raises an interesting question: how do I know this document is true? That's what this whole unit is about. All these lessons are going to walk you through it. How do we know the Bible is true? How do we know that it's accurate? How do we know that it's reliable and authoritative?

paragraphs.heading: The circular argument
paragraphs.text: See, the problem is that often we get stuck in this loop where we ask the question, how do I know that the Bible is true? Well, then we say, that's because the Bible says so. Well, how do I know that the Bible says so? Well, because I know the Bible is true. And we just keep going in a circle, over and over and over again, and we never actually have anything exterior that helps us understand whether or not the Bible is actually true. We throw in there a little bit of, well, it's the inspired — I can't write — the inspired word of God. And therefore it must be true, and it must be because the Bible says so, because it's the inspired word of God, because we know it's true, and we go on and on that way.

How do I know, beyond all of those things, that this is true? How do I know that it's authoritative? How do I know that what's in these pages is actually going to teach me how to live the life that God has designed for me? That's what students need to know, and that's what we're going to explore. In this first week, we're going to talk about text — and specifically this text, the New Testament. Now, last week we ended by talking about Jesus, and all that Jesus said, and all that Jesus claimed to be, and the resurrection, all this stuff about Jesus. How do I know that what's in here about Jesus in the New Testament is accurate?

paragraphs.heading: Autographs and manuscripts
paragraphs.text: Well, what's fascinating about that is that we have what's called an autograph and a manuscript. An autograph is an original copy. It's as if I actually gave my autograph, my signature. It's original to me. I wrote it, and only I can write it. That's essentially what we're talking about when we say an autograph. When we talk about texts from antiquity — the ancient texts, those biblical times and earlier and all around that era — we have no autographs. We have nothing originally written by anybody in their physical hand. But what we do have is manuscripts, copies. Sometimes they are copies of a copy of a copy; that is entirely possible.

So the question we have to answer in this first lesson is this: do we have enough manuscripts, and do we have enough manuscripts that are accurate across all of the copies, to say that what's in here in my hand is an accurate representation of what Paul wrote, what Jesus said, what Peter wrote, and what actually happened during the days of Jesus?

paragraphs.heading: Documents that prove something
paragraphs.text: So to start this process, we ask students in the introduction activity to look up a legal document that proves their existence. Think about it: you have a birth certificate, you have a driver's license, you can't get on an airplane without a driver's license or a passport. You're often asked for your Social Security card any time your identity is checked for a job or that kind of thing, right? So you have to have some kind of proof of your existence, proof that you are who you say you are. We have these legally binding documents that are proof of something. So we want students to start to see that there are documents out there even today that have this kind of power.

All right, so I want you to think about your students' textbooks in school, especially the ones that talk about ancient literature. Think of a world history textbook that's going to talk about the details of the ancient Roman Empire, Alexander the Great, some of the great armies, the movement of barbarian tribes — those kinds of things that help shape the history of the modern world, all of the things that your students learn and really consider to be actual fact. All of those things are derived from historical texts and from different things that give us clues into understanding what happened in history.

So, for instance, you have things like Natural History, by a historian named Pliny. Now, this guy was a Roman historian, and most of what he wrote about had to do with agriculture and business and economics and those kinds of things. But it gives us great insight into what Rome was like, and how to understand the Roman Empire, and some of the insights we have into their world and their technology as an ancient culture. All right. So we have not a ton of copies. It's estimated that we have roughly 100 or so — maybe less, maybe more — of something like that. And those are copies of a copy of a copy, sometimes in different languages, scattered throughout different places, those kinds of things.

Now, how much of the New Testament do we have? How much of the actual New Testament? This isn't full Bibles. I don't want you to think this is a bunch of actual full Bible copies. Sometimes they're just little pieces, little fragments, little things that we have to place together. Sometimes they're full books. Sometimes they're multiple books together.
