But oftentimes these are scattered all throughout the region, from the east to the west, and they're found in all kinds of different places and times. So if you put all of that together, we have roughly in excess of six thousand copies of just the New Testament. And if you put a whole bunch of other things together, you're talking in excess of 20,000 different copies. That's a lot of copies.

Now, what happens if you say, well, how accurate are these copies? Because that's going to help us understand how accurate this is. If you put all the copies together, everything across the board is in excess of 95 percent the same. And that three to five percent is words like "the" and "a," things that may have been missing or may have been taken out — but none of it affects theology. Now, that's pretty astounding. And in your leader guide, we're giving you resources to find out some more detailed and exact numbers. I would encourage you to check those out.

Josh McDowell has actually just updated some of those numbers, and some of these have even gotten better and better over the last couple of years. So I would encourage you to check those out and share those numbers with your students, because it's almost mind-bending to think that the New Testament, as it is here, is actually more reliable and more historical than some of the stuff that's in the textbooks your students are reading and learning in school as fact. Now, I'm not saying those aren't fact. But how much more reliable is the New Testament than some of the world history books we have in schools? It's a lot more reliable. This is huge, right?

paragraphs.heading: Misconception and illumination
paragraphs.text: So I do want to make one comment about the misconception and illumination, because what we've done here is slightly different from what we've done in the past. Before, the misconception was often a verse or a comment that was frequently misunderstood by students, and we wanted to point them in a direction that corrects them but also illuminates their understanding further. This year, what we did is we wanted to pull out some information from some other authors — some notable atheists and some people who don't agree with what Christianity teaches.

So you'll notice very specifically that this week we have Bart Ehrman. He is a New Testament critic and an agnostic who probably was a Christian. He understands the Bible very, very well, but he writes specifically against what the Bible teaches, and says that the Bible is not accurate. He says that we have only error-ridden copies, and that the vast majority of these are centuries removed from the originals and different from them, evidently in thousands of ways. Well, what's fascinating about that is that Bart Ehrman says that, but what we just talked about here clearly contradicts it.

So it's important — we bring this up specifically so that you can help your students navigate some of these things, because these are not obscure authors and people you never hear of. These are mainstream people in the media, sometimes on TV, often featured in National Geographic and Discovery Channel kinds of specials, where your students may come across them in the future. And we want you to be aware, so you can help make them aware, so they can say, well, you know what, let me look at these kinds of comments critically — so that they understand that just because someone like this says this, that doesn't necessarily make it true, and so that they make sure they dive into the actual evidence. If you read on in what Bart Ehrman says — super smart guy — he doesn't really back comments like this up with a whole bunch of evidence.

One resource that I do want to point out is that Jonathan Morrow wrote an excellent book called Questioning the Bible: 11 Major Challenges to the Bible's Authority, a suggested resource inside the leader's guide. So I would suggest that you pick that up yourself, but that book is designed specifically to speak to your students. So if your students have questions about this topic specifically, if they're just stuck and you need to move on, or if they just want to know more, encourage them — or maybe you just buy it for them. Get this book and have them read through it, and then set up a different discussion on that book specifically, and it'll be a tremendous resource for them.

So if we're getting what we believe from the Bible, then we had better be sure that what the Bible says is saying it accurately. And although it may seem that we have thousands of different kinds of translations, and we have so many copies — the Bible is the best-selling book in the history of the world, and it's been copied so many times, over and over and over and over again — and although there are lots of people trying to discredit it, when you continue to look at the evidence, the Bible continues to prove itself as something that has been transmitted over the course of history accurately and reliably to what was actually recorded originally.

paragraphs.heading: What that means for us
paragraphs.text: So you can be confident, and you can remind your students, as you sit in small group and encourage them and help them understand, that what Paul wrote and what Jesus said is actually what Paul wrote and what Jesus said. Now, that has incredible consequences, right? Either we listen to what Paul says and what Jesus says and what Peter says, and all that went on, and the gospel and the Old Testament and all that's going on in here — or we don't. But we can't assume that this is inaccurate.

So as you're getting into your small groups, talk with your students about this. Now that they understand that there's a reliability to this — and we're going to get even more into it in the next couple of weeks here — start to poke a little bit at them and say, well, what's this going to mean down the road? What's this going to mean today? What's this going to mean tomorrow, and next week, and in the next couple of weeks? The more you discover about the importance of this book, what is that going to mean for your life? Because the more you know about this, the less you can ignore it.

paragraphs.heading: The signature activity
paragraphs.text: This week we're talking about archaeology, and in the introduction activity we asked your students to produce their signature — kind of a strange thing to do, right? So, do your signature. There's my mess of a signature, and we asked them to do that multiple times. Well, why? Because when an archaeologist is digging — and what archaeologists do is, if you have an excavation site, you have to dig below. Well, what happens when a city falls? It crumbles to the ground; it all falls in.

It's not like today, where if this whole entire building came down, we would clear the rubble, send it to recycling facilities, rebuild, level the ground and start all over again. They didn't have those capabilities. So if a city fell and all the rubble sat here, they would simply level off the rubble and build a new city right on top. And they kept doing that year after year after year, or decade after decade, or whatever the case may be.

So as archaeologists are digging, they're digging below each of these levels. Each one is called — it's an archaeological tell, is what they call it. And they're digging into, well, they have to use clues to figure out that if they started digging here and found something, that's going to be from a different time period than if they dug down here and found something.

So the signature is a way to help your students understand that if they found a piece of paper with my signature on it, and they figured out that it was me with this big mess of a signature, they would know that — let's see — based on the fact that I used an Expo marker, the fact that I'm on a whiteboard, the fact that it's black, all these factors, plus the fact that they would connect it to me, they could figure out roughly the date, or at least get close to when this actually happened. Let me give you another example.

paragraphs.heading: A Lego illustration
paragraphs.text: This is the Hulkbuster, and full disclosure, this is mine, not my kids'. If this whole building collapsed — let's say we were in ancient times and they had Legos in ancient times — and this whole building collapsed, and they found pieces of this and put it back together and discovered that it was this, then based on the kind of Lego this is, based on the character, the fact that this is Iron Man in the Hulkbuster suit, they would pretty much know exactly when this Lego came out, roughly when it got built, and what era they're currently digging in.

So that's the importance, and that's kind of what archaeologists do. We want your students to start thinking about what that looks like. This isn't necessarily Indiana Jones kind of stuff, but it gives us a good idea of how this is done. So when they come across biblical artifacts, what does that mean for the biblical text?

paragraphs.heading: Finding a storyteller
paragraphs.text: For your storyteller, this is a really cool opportunity to have someone come in. You don't have to have an archaeologist, and you don't have to have anybody who has made an amazing discovery. If you can, that would be awesome. If you happen to have somebody at a local seminary who has done some traveling to the Middle East and Jerusalem and whatnot, that would be awesome. But if not, that's okay — don't worry like you have to have that. You could simply have somebody who was rummaging around in grandma's attic and found a really important family heirloom.

Years ago, my grandma was moving from her condo to a long-term care facility, because she was getting ill and needed to be watched pretty much 24-7. So my family all got together and we were going through all of her stuff. That's a little bit weird when she's sitting there watching us go through all of her stuff. But it was fascinating, because we found all these really cool artifacts, and there were stories behind them. It was stuff that reminded my dad of his childhood and of what that meant, and we talked about really interesting stories and had a really great time walking down those memories.

But if you could just find a storyteller to even tell that story, it helps connect the importance of discovery and archaeology and artifacts and all those pieces of history with what we can know about the Bible. Because my dad can tell me a story, but when he connects it with an artifact or something from his past, that story becomes that much more reliable — because otherwise it could just be that he remembered it wrong. It also becomes that much more powerful, because I'm understanding that what he's telling me is now actually history. And that's exactly what we're hoping your students get when they look at archaeology and Scripture.

paragraphs.heading: Small group focus
paragraphs.text: So for small groups, your focus is simple. I want you to focus on helping students see that this Bible is also history. Yes, it's the Word of God. Yes, it's inspired. Yes, it's completely accurate in every way, because God made it that way. But God also made this an accurate reflection of history. What goes on in here is actually historical.

We have found coins that give us indication that David actually was a king. And we've seen things from the New Testament that have the inscription of Pontius Pilate on them, reminding us that Pontius Pilate was an actual person. He was an actual governor. He actually was the one responsible during Jesus's crucifixion. There is history behind it all.

paragraphs.heading: Be ready for questions
paragraphs.text: We want your students to drill that in, but I also want you to pay attention to their questions. Now that they're starting to see Scripture as something a little bit more important than maybe they thought it was, there's going to be some pushback, and some thought that, well, isn't this just a bunch of stories and myths that maybe people thought were true? And there's some sort of evidence that maybe they just messed around with history, and they just messed around with the truth a little bit. There are going to be questions, and you need to be ready to answer those questions and talk through them a little bit.

paragraphs.heading: One final question
paragraphs.text: But I want you to continue to walk students down that road of helping them understand and see the importance of this book and what it means for their lives. So I'm going to leave you with one final question that I want you to leave your students with. Two weeks in, what does this information, from biblical reliability to archaeological evidence, do for how you see the Bible?

Think about that for yourself, because if you didn't know some of this information prior to these last couple of weeks, and now you're moving forward with your students — think about that with yourself. Does this change how you see it? And don't be afraid to share this with your students and help them see, hey, I didn't know either. Maybe I didn't know all of this. This is new information for you as well. Share that with your students.

Walk alongside them, and especially encourage your small group leaders to do the same thing, so that they can see that this isn't something they ought to know, that everybody should know, and they're just kind of out of the loop — this is a journey for all of you. And the more you understand, the greater this book becomes.

paragraphs.heading: Prophecy is tricky
paragraphs.text: All right — prophecy. Now think of it this way. If the Bible is both accurate and trustworthy, and we can know it to be true, and we can also know it to be historical, what then does that say about prophecy? Prophecy is tricky. It's almost as if we can believe that the Bible is accurate history. We can show that; it's concrete, and it lines up with some other things.

We can show that the Bible is completely accurate across all of history, and that it is 95% the same exact thing that Jesus actually said, or whatever. Prophecy is trickier, because prophecy can be something that you might just discount: "Well, that just sort of was happenstance," or "that was just coincidence, and it just happened that way." Or maybe it was manufactured to look like it was a fulfillment of prophecy.

paragraphs.heading: Walking through this week
paragraphs.text: So here's the deal with this week. As you go through it piece by piece, as you walk students through the misconceptions and the illuminations, as you walk your students through and help guide them through their introduction activity and their exploration of Isaiah chapters 52 and 53, as you look at the questions and start to piece this whole week together, I want you to keep one thing in mind this week — and that's it.

paragraphs.heading: When the questions come
paragraphs.text: This week could be a difficult week. This could be the week — one of those weeks when students start firing all kinds of questions at you, especially your small group leaders. So here's what we're going to do. We're going to write the questions down, and we're going to dig in and do some research. And I want you to come back, if you have to, and even take an additional week to answer those questions.

Don't pretend like you have all the answers. Now, you might have a bunch of the answers, and that's awesome. But if you don't, don't pretend, and don't brush it off, because we're sort of at that moment now where you probably have students who — especially if they started out very skeptical — are hopefully walking closer and closer and closer. But the closer you get, the easier it is to just fall off the edge.

Because if we discount a question, the train may just come off the rails, and it's maybe over. I don't know. So you want to approach these kinds of things very carefully. You've spent so much time and energy developing authentic and organic community, and trust with these students, and openness and honesty, and being able to ask the difficult questions. Now is one of those times when the difficult questions are going to start to come. When it comes to prophecy, there just may be those kinds of things.

I can't predict what kind of questions your students may ask, but from my experience, this is always one of those areas that just pops up. So if you don't know the answers, or your small group leaders don't know the answers, write them down, gather together, get some answers, bring your students back together, and give them the answers that they're seeking.

paragraphs.heading: The misconception this week
paragraphs.text: So for this week, don't be afraid to directly address the misconception. Here's how we've worded it: it seems to be entirely impossible for one man to fulfill hundreds of prophecies, not to mention that the way Jesus fulfilled Messianic prophecy was very much contrary to popular Jewish theology. Jewish leaders were looking for the coming Messiah to be a political, military and spiritual ruler who would dethrone foreign rule and reestablish Israel as a world superpower. Instead, Jesus unexpectedly established his spiritual kingdom. It's a worldview shift that has prevented many from accepting Him as Savior.

Keep that in mind. This is a complete worldview shift for many. It was that way for Jews in the first century, and it's that way probably for many of your students as well. Don't be afraid to hit the bell.

paragraphs.heading: What this lesson asks
paragraphs.text: Lesson number four: authority. This lesson is basically a response. It's invoking a response from your students of this: if the Bible is all that we've said the Bible is so far, then now what? Because the Bible clearly has something to say that's really, really important, and it has some authority over our lives. So now what?

paragraphs.heading: Choosing the storyteller
paragraphs.text: So let's start with the storyteller. The storyteller could be — and this week I would suggest it be — a student. I would ask your students who has been greatly impacted over the last couple of weeks. I would ask them, hey, who has really just had their mind completely blown and needs to get it off their chest about what this means, because now they're going to have a changed life, moving in the direction that God desires.

Maybe that's in connection with a retreat, or with a specific moment in their life. But if you've got a student like that, then I would highly encourage you to use that, because what happens in these kinds of moments is that it's really easy for an adult to say, this book is important, you should follow it. Well, they're still learning this book, as many of us are as well. And it's hard for them to really grasp: okay, what parts do I follow, and how do I follow, and what's literal and what's not?

There are just so many other things here that they often look at us adults and think, yeah, but you've got it figured out and you can do it. I don't need that right now. I'm young and I can do what I want. When I'm your age, maybe I'll do that. I get that it's important, and I'll get there. It's more powerful if one of their peers stands up and declares, based on the evidence, based on what we've studied, based on the conviction of the Holy Spirit: I believe this book to be authoritative, and I'm going to respond in that way and make sure my life is headed down the path that God wants it to go. That's a powerful, powerful statement, and a powerful storyteller, if they can recall how that happened.

And you might have other students, and maybe that is happening to them and they either don't realize it or aren't willing to speak up about it. That might conjure up some other feelings from some other students and give you a little bit of a gauge of where you're at. If you don't have a student in that space, then I would suggest that maybe you have a graduate — someone who has gone through your program and is now in college. Now that things are kind of rolling along and they've been in college for a little bit of time, maybe they're starting to experience some things, maybe they're starting to see the importance of what's in here, especially with some of the contradictions they may be hearing on the college campus. Have them come in and talk about the Bible's authority and fill that storyteller role.

paragraphs.heading: The objections you'll hear
paragraphs.text: Okay, so we say it all the time and we hear it all the time, right? The Bible is the word of God. And what we're saying is that the Bible is inspired. The Bible is infallible. The Bible is the word of God. Everything in it is absolutely true. Therefore, it must be authoritative, right? But what students will often struggle with, and what you'll hear in terms of objections, is this: that the Bible was written by men.

Wait a minute, how can the Bible be authoritative? And yeah, okay, sure, it can be historical, and okay, yeah, it can fulfill prophecy, and okay, it can be completely accurate in some kind of strange way. But how can it be so authoritative that we call it the word of God? That we call it the very commands of God, handed down from him to us so that we can live the way he has designed us to live — if it was written by men?

How do we know that when Matthew recorded the words of Jesus, he actually recorded the words of Jesus? I mean, I probably wouldn't get it right. I was listening to our sermon just on Sunday, and I tried to write down exactly what the pastor said, because I really liked what he said in one particular sentence — and I couldn't remember exactly what he said in that moment. How could we expect Matthew to write down everything that Jesus said perfectly? These are the kinds of objections that you will get from your students.

And it's not a terribly difficult objection to deal with, but just to kind of paint the picture for you, the way I've done it with students in the past is this: think of it this way. I'm not making an exact equation, but it helps paint a better picture. You have Jesus, and you have the Bible. Now, clearly we don't treat the Bible the same way we treat Jesus. However, we very easily say that Jesus is 100% man and he's also 100% God. Now wait a minute — if I can comfortably say that, why can't I comfortably say that the Bible was written by men, inspired by God, to be completely accurate? See, if God can make this sort of thing happen, God can make this sort of thing happen. It's pretty simple.

The second objection you'll often hear students make is that the Bible may be accurate and historical and all of those things, but that the Bible is simply a book about God — that it's man's recordings of who God is, or of who they thought him to be. Now, that's not accurate either, because if the Bible is authoritative, then sure, it's what we think about God, but it was completely accurate about who God actually is. Because otherwise we don't know who God really is. But we do know who God really is, because he came in Jesus, so we actually do have that picture. So this is so your students start to see that, although it seems very easy to say other things about the Bible — things which really just allow us to excuse ourselves on various types of sin — what the Bible teaches is 100% authoritative.

paragraphs.heading: In your small groups
paragraphs.text: So in your small groups, as you're thinking through all these things, think through the implications of what all of this means. These last four weeks, what is all of this coming to? What conclusions are your students now coming to? And I want you to remember three specific things that your students can understand in order to know truth through all of this. One, they should have a greater appreciation for this, right? So if nothing else, they should have a greater appreciation for the Bible — what it says, what it teaches, how it came together, all of those pieces — and hopefully that will compel them to read a little bit more.

Secondly, that they'll be more inclined to read this. How many Christians have read the Bible cover to cover multiple times? It's the greatest book, the greatest, biggest-selling, best-selling book in the history of the world, and probably the least read book in the history of the world. And I think they're more likely to follow. The more they appreciate, the more they'll read; the better they'll follow. That is the aim of this week.

paragraphs.heading: Into everyday conversation
paragraphs.text: Now, this has to sort of cross into — we're going to start talking in the next few weeks here about what this means in conversation. When your students are in college, when your students are talking with friends, and they might be sitting reading this and someone makes a comment: how do they then defend and talk intelligently about this biblical text? And I think over the last four weeks we've been able to provide the tools that our students need to be able to talk intelligently about what this book is all about.

paragraphs.heading: Take a breath and pray
paragraphs.text: I want you to take a second and just take a deep breath. We are going to be talking about evil and pain and suffering. This may seem like it's just another lesson in the full gamut of lessons, and you may be tired. The year is coming to an end, and this is going to take some tenacity to get through. I want you to pray, and I want you to pray for the next four weeks for your students. Not that you haven't been already, but if it's been hit or miss, I want you to really dial in on prayer this coming week and in these next couple of weeks.

Not only do you probably have students who are coming along and maybe are on the verge of making some decisions — I pray that that is the case — but you also have students who are going to have some significant questions, doubts, pain and hurt brought up these next few weeks. I want you to be aware of that before we even get started: we're going to dive into some pretty deep and some pretty heavy things over the next couple of weeks. I want you to be ready for it. So as you prepare for this week's discussion on evil, I want you to be prayerful for yourself, for your students and for your leaders.

paragraphs.heading: Two approaches to evil
paragraphs.text: When we're talking about evil, we're actually talking about two different approaches to how we talk about evil, and throughout the next couple of weeks we're going to look at both of these approaches. I want you to be patient, because there are two different ways that we can do this. There is what we call — what I call — the philosophical. Why can't I spell? We'll just call it that. The second is the pastoral approach. Now, the philosophical approach is sort of academic, and the pastoral approach is just what it is: it's pastoral.

So we're going to look at it from both sides. I want you to make sure that you understand that at the starting gate, so you don't jump the gun. It's important that we see it from both sides, but not every student is going to respond to it from both sides, which is why we do it this particular way.

paragraphs.heading: What evil actually is
paragraphs.text: In this first lesson, we want students to really understand what evil is. Evil is the opposite of good. It's the opposite of God. A lot of people will sort of assert that evil is this thing that maybe God created — that maybe God did something where, as part of the whole created universe, there is this force called evil, and it's the opposite of good: good's a thing and evil's a thing. But evil is the absence of good. It's a privation of good. It's sort of the same thing as darkness. We don't have a measurement for darkness; the measurement is light, and darkness is what we call the absence of light.

The same thing works for cold and heat. We don't have a measurement for cold. We have a measurement for the absence of heat, and that's what we call cold. We call it the absence of heat; we call it cold. It's just how we describe it. Evil is the same way. You remove God from the picture, you remove his goodness from the picture, and suddenly you have what we would call evil. So, very philosophically and kind of heady, the idea is that evil is this sort of other-than-God-ness out there that humanity is responsible for. And we're responsible since the garden, because we actually allowed evil to permeate our world by making the wrong choice. We made a choice to remove God from the picture.

So evil is a stark, dark reminder that we've lost our way — that we've looked to ourselves for our own moral compass, that we've told God we've got this figured out and we don't need him. So, being the gracious God that he is, he said: you have free will. You can do what you want. You can choose to go your own way. So we did. And evil was the result of that choice.

paragraphs.heading: The compass illustration
paragraphs.text: One way I think your students can really grasp this idea is through the storyteller. You want someone who can tell a great story about being lost. For some of them, it might not be too hard to find someone who has been lost but didn't use navigation. We all have. I don't remember the last time I actually got lost, because all I have to do is plug it into here. But what if you had to navigate by the sun or by a compass?

So you have north, and then you have south, and you have west, and you have east. How do I know if I need to head east? How do I know which way is east? Well, the only way in which I know where east is is if I know where north is. So the first thing you do when you're lost and you have a compass, or you can look at the sun, is figure out where north is. Once you find what's called magnetic north, then you can orient yourself and you can figure out every other direction.

Well, imagine if the compass just kept being pointed back to you. What would you do? You'd just be walking in circles, trying to figure out where you're supposed to go. You'd never be able to find east or west or south, for that matter. It has to be something external of you, something that's not you, to do that. So God serves as that moral compass.

paragraphs.heading: Evil points to God
paragraphs.text: So what that leads us to conclude — and this is where the philosophical piece comes in — is that the very fact that evil exists suggests that God exists. Think of it this way. If there is no good, then there is no evil. If there's no God, there's no good. If there's no good, there's no evil. And if there's no good, then there's no evil — which means there's nothing to compare it to. The only way in which we understand what evil is is because we have good, because we can look at evil and say, that's not good.

So if that doesn't exist, then God doesn't exist. But there is evil. Therefore, there's good. Therefore, there's the standard to which we compare good and evil. Therefore, God exists — that's kind of how that works. Hopefully that made sense. So from a philosophical standpoint, the very existence of evil suggests that God exists, because we have a standard by which we can understand what evil actually is.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: Okay, so, small group time. You're going to get questions, and it's going to get real, real fast. This is the point where students are going to start bringing up probably a load of questions on you, like, well, why does God allow suffering? Why does God allow good people to suffer? Why do bad things happen to good people? And any other variation of the question that basically says, why is there evil and suffering? Some of it you can probably answer as it relates to evil specifically. Some of it you may want to table. But be careful how you table a question. Make sure you write it down — in your leader's guide, your discussion guide, or wherever you have to — so you can come back to it and so you don't ignore the question.

But there are going to be a lot of questions. And if you're not getting a lot of questions, your students still have the questions. So I would suggest posing them yourself. Ask them the questions that they're probably asking you. So if no one says, why has God allowed suffering? Or why has God allowed good people to suffer? Why has God allowed a child to die? Why has God allowed a lot of things that we kind of look at and go, oh my gosh, what an injustice, what a terrible thing? You ask it, and see what they think. But be ready, because this is going to start getting very, very personal and very deep for some students, especially if they have experienced any kind of evil or suffering in their lives.

paragraphs.heading: A common atheist objection
paragraphs.text: So, 7.2 — we call it falsehood. This lesson really is a response to a common atheist objection: that if God were so big and mighty and powerful and sovereign and all good, then he would have prevented evil. He wouldn't have allowed it in the first place. I mean, think about it: if God can do these things, if God can just speak and suddenly we have a universe, then why can't he prevent evil?

Years ago I did a debate with an atheist, and this was essentially his argument. His argument was pretty complex, but let me summarize it as quickly as I can. He basically said that if God existed, God would have created a world in which only God-like objects existed, and he called that God-world. And if this God-world were an actual world, then all the pieces of God-world would be just like God. There would be no suffering, there would be no evil, there would be nothing at all. Everything would be absolutely perfect, on an equal playing field with God.

My response was pretty simple. It took me some time to figure out exactly what he was saying, and then it hit me. I said, "First, why do you think this is the case?" And he said, "Well, because there's evil and suffering in the world." I said, "Let's put that aside for a second. Is there anything that God cannot do?" And he said, "Well, if God is all-powerful, then there's nothing that God cannot do. That's why, if he can't prevent evil, then God must not exist." I said, "That's not the case. Just because God is all-powerful and sovereign and omniscient and all-awesome, does that mean there's nothing that God cannot do?"

So, unfortunately, the old song — "my God is so great, my God is so big, there's nothing…" — is actually not necessarily true. Because God could not create a world in which only God-like objects, or God-like things that are equivalent to him, existed. Because if that were the case, then God would not exist, because he wouldn't be God anymore. He would just be equal to everything else; everything would be the same as God, and all things would be God, and that would take us into a form of pantheism. So his argument didn't work.

paragraphs.heading: God is not responsible for evil
paragraphs.text: But there's this understanding of, well, why wouldn't God do that? Simply put, there are some things that God actually cannot do. And what's important about this lesson is to help students understand that God is not the one who is responsible for evil. God did not create it. As I said last week, it's not a thing to be created, because evil is not a thing. God did not create it; God is not responsible. And although God is doing something to remedy the situation, he still has to allow us to have free will to make our own choices.

paragraphs.heading: What God cannot do
paragraphs.text: So this week, I would get your students thinking about the character and nature of who God is. Have them think about it, just like in the intro activity, where we ask them about things that are impossible for humanity to do — but what about things that are impossible for God to do? What are some other things that maybe God cannot do? Have your students think that through: what makes God God, and what limits does God actually have?

Now, I don't mean fun things like "Can God create a rock so big he can't lift it?" and strange questions like that. That's not what I'm talking about. I mean things like this: God cannot contradict himself. God cannot lie. So have your students think that through, to help paint a better picture of the nature of God and of exactly what he's doing in this world to remedy the evil and the suffering that is so prevalent.

paragraphs.heading: Morally justified reasons
paragraphs.text: So God has morally justified reasons for allowing the temporary existence of evil and suffering in our world. That may seem like a cop-out — like, what, that's the best you've got? But remember what Scripture says, what Paul says in 1 Corinthians: we only see things in part right now. We don't have the full picture. There's still quite a bit of mystery going on.

The example I always used to give my students was the example of being a kid, or of parenting my own kids. I may know what's best for my kids. They may not realize that I know what's best, and what I'm telling them they have to do, or what I'm putting them through, may seem like a terrible, terrible thing for them in that moment. The whole world is coming crashing down on them, and yet I know exactly what I'm doing, and it's for their good. That may be the case sometimes. And sometimes it's just the case that evil is evil, and evil just happens. God doesn't like it any more than we do, but he has to allow it, even if only for a time.

And as we'll see later on, when we get to more of the pastoral approach to this question of evil, it can be used for something exceptionally good. So in your small groups, I want you to start to brainstorm a little bit about what good can come from evil. But I also want you to be very aware — I keep beating this drum — very aware of the questions that are coming. If the questions didn't come last week, they may be coming this week, and they may be coming next week. They may be coming all of the weeks.

paragraphs.heading: Know your students
paragraphs.text: And be aware of some of the things that your students are going through. By now you probably know your students really well. You probably know their families, you've probably talked with their parents, and you've connected with their families on some level. Do your best to be aware of some of the things that your students are going through, for two reasons. One, so that you can pray with them, and pastor them along, and walk with them, and be there for them in the way that you need to be. That goes without saying.

But the other is that when we're dealing with these kinds of issues, you want to have an awareness and a sensitivity so that you don't say anything that would touch the wrong nerve with your students. Sometimes you may want to a little bit, to get a response out of students and to move them along, but you also want to be very, very aware of where they are, so that you can minister to them in the best possible way without setting them back at all.

paragraphs.heading: Look to him for hope
paragraphs.text: So rather than going down the easy road and simply doubting God because of the evil that we see around us, we can actually look to him for hope. We can know that he has a plan, know that he has a purpose, and know that of all the things we're going through, it's not for nothing. We can look to him for significant hope.

paragraphs.heading: A book that stirred controversy
paragraphs.text: Several years ago I was teaching one of my Bible classes when a really important and significant book in the lives of most evangelical Christians came out. It created a firestorm of conversation, waves of controversy, and all kinds of things happening in the Christian world. The book was Love Wins by Rob Bell, and I had all kinds of parents asking me if we were going to read it, or demanding that we don't read it. I had students asking me about it, so I finally said enough is enough — I need to figure out what the story is. So I read it, and I used it as a discussion point for my students.

The book had an incredible way of bringing up some really, really important topics to discuss. But what was interesting was that the students seemed to really gravitate toward what the book was suggesting: that we somehow have this endless chance-after-chance cycle of getting to God; that if we miss it the first time, we'll get a second try at it; and that the idea of hell is really not all that accurate. It's an interesting conversation piece, and something that we ought to talk about.

paragraphs.heading: The Bible is clear
paragraphs.text: But the Bible is pretty clear. We've talked about the reliability of this text, and Jesus is really clear that hell exists. Yet it's so easy for our students to want to discount that, because we don't necessarily want to be held accountable for our actions, and we don't really want to face the consequences. Who wants to face consequences? So the question I'm often asked is, okay, well, what is hell like? I don't know. It's probably not nice. I don't really know. I don't know if I want to know. It's not God. Hell is the tragic consequence of rejecting God.

paragraphs.heading: Imagining what hell is like
paragraphs.text: To help your students understand what this tragic consequence would be like, the intro experience takes them through a mini journey of imagining the best possible place — their favorite place. Why do you love it? Describe it. Even put pictures in there. And then remove all of its goodness, everything. Cross out any word that has good meaning. Remove all benefits from that place, all value, all joy, all refreshing qualities, all of it. What would that place be like then? That should help them get into that space of what hell would be like.

I often describe it to students this way. Common grace is the grace that God provides all of us, right? The fact that God is sustaining this world, every breath that I take, the sun that is shining, the air that is blowing, the trees growing, all the rain that falls, all of the things that happen on the righteous and the unrighteous — those are all common grace, because God is here, active and moving in history, and participating in sovereignly taking care of this world.

Now remove all of that. God is not doing any of that. Can you imagine what it might be like to not be able to take a breath, to not have the sun shining, to not have this earth sustained by Him? Uninhabitable. That's the way I try to paint a picture of hell for students, to give them that sense of, oh, God is doing all of this for me whether I choose Him or not, right?

paragraphs.heading: Does God send people to hell?
paragraphs.text: So then the question comes: well, wait a minute, how come God sends good people to hell? How come God sends anybody to hell? The short answer is that God doesn't send anybody — we send ourselves, because we choose to not want Him. I've often said that God honors our choices and allows us to choose not Him, and then gives us that very choice.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: So this week, small groups as always — but this week especially is super important, because all that we're talking about is going to come to a bit of a culmination. How can a God who we've already said is good be allowing evil and all those kinds of things, and how can He then have the existence of hell alongside that? If God is so good and so loving and He allows this kind of evil — and this is the question that has been posed to me several times — if God allows evil and allows the suffering to happen, and He's so good, then why would He have hell as a punishment for not believing? It almost seems like there's a contradiction. These are some of the questions that your students may bring up, or some version of them.

Again, open discussion. It's okay. If a student is not sure about hell, invite the discussion, invite the dialogue. Don't shoot them down and just point to Scripture and thump on the Bible like, well, this is what the Bible says. Well, yes — and we've talked about the reliability of the text and the authority of what's in there. But hell is a very, very real reality that can be difficult for some people to deal with. So be patient with your students as you bring them along if they're not quite there yet. Allow them the time to process it. And small groups are going to be one of those times where that happens.

And again, it's understanding that God wants us to choose Him. God wants us to be with Him. God invites us into relationship; He does not force us. And that is love in action: I want you to be with me. Imagine being married to somebody you love who doesn't love you back. That doesn't seem to make any sense.

paragraphs.heading: Closing encouragement
paragraphs.text: Well, you made it through this week, and you've almost made it through the rest of the year. We continue to pray for you here, and we continue to pray for your students. I hope that this process of looking at hell and evil and suffering in a very, very real way has helped your students understand not only the point of suffering but the character of God a little bit better — and not only that this points to the existence of God in some sort of philosophical sense, but that even in the midst of suffering God is right there with us, feeling the pain along with us. I hope your students have a better picture of who God is and who Christ is, and what their salvation means, and all of that.

You have four more lessons to go. Now would be a good time to take another inventory of your students and where they are. Go back to some of your original notes about how your students started off this year and how they were around Unit 4. Where are they now? You've got some students who have made some decisions — I hope and pray that you have. Do you have some students who still have significant questions? If you need to, take some time and revisit some of those questions, either as a group, individually, or in small groups — wherever you need to. Don't rush this process. You've got four lessons to go, all of which are going to focus on wrapping things up and tying up some loose ends, and helping to send your students onward and forward into the world with greater conviction, greater confidence, and greater courage.

paragraphs.heading: Talking about love again
paragraphs.text: You might be thinking that we're talking about love again, and your students might look at it and think, "We're talking about love again." Well, we're going to keep talking about love, because love is so important. Paul said it in 1 Corinthians, right? If we have all this stuff, if we're this amazing person and we can do all these amazing things, but we don't have love, then it's all for nothing.

So we want to make sure that we talk about love. At this point, you and your students have walked through an incredible amount of information. In fact, they're so much more intelligent and, hopefully, confident in their conviction for what we as Christians believe. It's exciting to think, when I look back at this book, about all the things they've studied and that you have gone through. It's really, really exciting to think back to even just where we started from.

paragraphs.heading: The temptation to be right
paragraphs.text: But it's also really easy, after you've been through all of this, to have so much knowledge crammed into your head. You might have — and I hope you have — students who are really excited to share what has now been crammed into their heads, and hopefully in ways that their hearts have been changing and have been incredibly impacted by what you've studied over the last several months. And yet, instead of sharing that with love, sometimes we get caught up in trying to be right. Sometimes we get caught up in trying to get notches in our spiritual belt. Sometimes we get caught up in trying just to win the argument and to beat down on somebody else's beliefs or somebody else's faith.

paragraphs.heading: Love and humility
paragraphs.text: That's not how we want to do it. So we wanted to make sure that we took time out to communicate the idea of communicating your faith to others in love and in humility. That can be really difficult to do. It can be difficult to train someone to sit back and actually take the time to listen, to take the time to be interested in what somebody else says, to take the time to really be just like Jesus.

So that's really what this lesson is all about. We want your students — just like we put inside the introduction activity — to think about what it looks like and what it feels like at a time when they actually experienced love. We want them to go back into that moment, so that they understand what they felt like, and so that they understand how others ought to feel when they express love of some kind to another person.

paragraphs.heading: Going off script with role-playing
paragraphs.text: So for this week, I'm going to take you a little bit off script — and maybe for next week as well. I want you to work on something. I want you to work on role-playing. It's not necessarily what's inside here, but after walking with you through this process, I sat back and thought that I really feel like you need to do some good quality role-playing now. That might be between two students, that might be between you and another student, or another adult leader and a student. But the idea here is that it's a teachable moment.

You want to show students what it looks like to engage in a conversation with another person in love. But you also want to show students what it looks like to engage another person in conversation without love. They need to see both. Even if you have two students, and one of them is displaying something that's good, maybe one of them is displaying something that's not so good. Don't ridicule them, but use this as a teaching moment so that they can see it, because some students are just bent toward arguing.

I've had students over the years who, no matter what you do and no matter how you say that they're trying to be loving, they just want to argue and they just want to win. And other students don't want to argue at all — they just want to be agreeable. Based on different students' personalities, they need to see a couple of different things. So involve as many students as you can, get them role-playing a little bit, and use those things as teachable moments, so your students can get a feel for what that looks like and feels like before they ever go out into any kind of conversation.

paragraphs.heading: They're going to mess up
paragraphs.text: But they are going to go out into conversation. I hope they go out and have conversations — but remind them that they're going to mess it up, and that's okay. They're going to come back and say, "Oh, I should have said this," and "Oh, I came off wrong," and "Oh, I said this wrong," or "I didn't think of this," or "I forgot that." It's okay. The fact that they remember those things afterward will continue to build their confidence, and they'll continue to get better and better and better.

Just like anything else, this is a skill that has to be developed. But encourage them to continue to use it. Encourage them, and find ways as a group to get out together, so that you can do things together and encourage each other and spur one another on. But make sure your students see exactly what love ought to look like, in as real a scenario as you can get.

paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.text: Okay, so small group. Small group time is going to be interesting, because what you have an opportunity to do this time is to talk with students about how they can love in different ways — maybe in ways they've never thought of. Depending on the dynamic of the particular group, they might not be able to think of love in the particular terms that another student can think of, so students need each other to bounce ideas back and forth. That way they can understand how it all will work in their particular situation. How one student perceives loving another person is going to be far different than maybe another student. So use your small group time as a way to open up that conversation, to really explore all the different ways that students can connect with other people in a way that Jesus would.

paragraphs.heading: Relationships, not conversions
paragraphs.text: Okay, so the last thing. We talk about love because love is what builds relationships. Please remember that it is so important to build relationships. Make sure your students understand that this is not about getting conversions — this is about building relationships. Jesus said to his disciples that it's by your love and by the way you treat one another that they'll know that you are my disciples, and that they'll know who I am. The way in which we love other people is how some people are only ever going to see Jesus. Don't focus on the conversions. Focus on the relationships, and focus on the ways in which we can love others.

paragraphs.heading: Going out is terrifying
paragraphs.text: Last week we talked about the need for love when we're engaging in conversation. We want to get out there, and we want to be loving to other people. But if you or any of your students are like me, that very concept is terrifying. It's the fact that I have to go out — not the love part, that's not so terrifying, but the part where you go out and actually have a conversation. That part is terrifying. I need a plan of attack. I am very introverted and very reserved, and I'm sure some of your students are too. I'm not all that good at small talk, at just having a conversation. In fact, I actively try to avoid small talk. I like to get to the point.

paragraphs.heading: When you can't answer
paragraphs.text: So when I'm entering a conversation about spiritual things, or when I want to advance a conversation and get to the gospel so that I can get to Jesus — because I want them to know who Jesus is — I need a plan of attack. But I'm sure that many of your students, and maybe you yourself, ask this, because I know I get there all the time: what happens when they ask you a question that you can't answer? Here is what happens in those moments. Somebody asks us a question.

We immediately want to have an answer, to come right back and say, "Yeah, I've got that answer, and I've got that answer," because we feel like if we have all of the answers, then we can somehow convince the other person that what we believe is absolutely right — we've got all the answers to all their questions. Well, nothing could be further from the truth. That's not at all the case. There are going to be times when we get stumped and we don't know what to say, or the person we're talking to has a belief system or a view on things that we're just not all that familiar with. You can't know everything about every single person.

paragraphs.heading: The art of asking questions
paragraphs.text: But there's a really simple strategy that I want you to add in and to talk about with your students: when they're engaged in a conversation, you want to make sure that you are asking questions. That's what this week is all about — the idea and the art of asking questions. Questions are so, so important. If we ask good questions, then we're probably going to get good answers. Just like any good teacher knows, you don't ask yes-or-no questions. You ask in-depth, probing questions — "why" kinds of questions — to draw out of people the answers that you want, the answers that you need.

The same holds true in our conversations. This especially works if you have no idea what the other person is talking about, because you can probe a little bit deeper and get them to talk it through. At the same time, you're giving off the idea — because you are, and because you want to be — that you're extremely interested in what they have to say. That goes back to last week, when we talked about love and building relationships and that sort of thing. So there are two specific questions that we can ask somebody if you get stumped.

paragraphs.heading: What do you mean by that?
paragraphs.text: The first question is simple: what do you mean by that? This question is used when you're really not sure what the person thinks, when the person says something that you're just not all that clear on. "I believe that Jesus is just a good moral teacher." What do you mean by that? You can probably guess what they might mean, but maybe that's not it at all. "God just doesn't exist, because there's too much evil in the world." Well, what do you mean by that? You can "what do you mean by that" people to death. You can go over and over and over again: what do you mean by that, or some variation of it.

It's a very simple question, but it does two things. First, it digs deeper into the person and what they're actually thinking. Second, it buys you time to think about what you want to say. It allows them to clarify what they're saying, so they can't just make a one-off statement to you, and it buys you a little bit of time to think through their opinion more thoroughly and more thoughtfully.

paragraphs.heading: How did you come to that?
paragraphs.text: The second question is: how did you come to that conclusion? Again, people make one-off statements all the time. How did they get there? So if they said something like, "God can't exist because there's too much evil in the world" — well, how do you come to that conclusion? There's a much larger explanation that I need for that. And you don't say it with an attitude; you say it as someone who is genuinely interested. How did you come to that conclusion? Really? I really want to know. I'm really interested in what you have to say.

What this does is help them see that you are actually interested in what they have to say, that you actually want to know what they think rather than just giving them what you think. There's a big difference between the two. And again, that's why last week and this week are connected together, because by doing this kind of thing you're showing them love, you're showing them relationship, you're showing that you care about them as a person and not just feeding them your opinion.

paragraphs.heading: The most valuable tool
paragraphs.text: The most valuable tool that you or your students have is the ability to sit down face-to-face with somebody and have a conversation. There are a lot of tips and tricks to sharing your faith, but the number one thing to keep in your toolbox is the ability to ask great questions and to engage in deep, meaningful conversations with another person. It does so much more than just give the gospel. It builds relationship, so that when that person finally receives Christ, discipleship can actually begin, rather than just a conversion.

paragraphs.heading: Why I walked away
paragraphs.text: Years ago, when I was a high school student, I walked away from Christianity and went down a whole other path for a good long time. The primary reason I walked away is that I had questions and I had doubts. You have gotten up to this point now where you not only have all this content — we've talked about love, we've talked about the power of questions and the power of conversation — but somewhere in there, at some point, questions from others, information from other people, going to college, all kinds of different things are going to come at your students, causing doubt. What happens when they doubt?

I walked away because I was doubting. I asked a question, and I was told not to ask the questions. I was told to just believe. I was told to just have faith, and I didn't even know what that meant. I couldn't figure it all out, so I said enough, and I walked away. The statistics are still out there, and they're still pretty prevalent, that a large majority of students leave youth group after high school. There are a whole bunch of reasons for that. One of them is that when they have doubts, those doubts aren't getting answered.

paragraphs.heading: Invite the doubts in
paragraphs.text: So this is an opportunity to open it up to your students and say, "Listen, I get it. I know you have doubts." Maybe share some of your own — and that's okay. Let's talk about them. Let's make sure this is an open forum. Weeks ago, at the very beginning of this process, we talked about the idea of having open communication and having a youth group that was very authentic and very open and invited the difficult questions. We talked about how those difficult questions were going to come. They're probably going to come even more now, because sometimes the more information you have, the more questions you have as a result.

So invite those in. Invite those doubts — whether students are not sure about Jesus, not sure about the existence of God, not sure about the biblical text, not sure about evil and pain and suffering, not sure about any of the things we've talked about, and maybe some things we haven't talked about, because there are a whole bunch of cultural issues that step into this that you have to help students navigate.

And that's where helping students navigate doubt is an incredibly important thing, an important tool at actually furthering their faith. Because as they get those things answered, as they feel free to express those doubts, that tells them that we as leaders understand, that we've been there, that it's okay, and that we're going to walk with them through those.

paragraphs.heading: Large group Q&A
paragraphs.text: So for the introduction activity this week, we asked students literally to write down one question they've been wrestling with. Now, as a large group activity, you might actually take and compile some of those. You might do a Q&A session. I find Q&A sessions to be incredibly helpful. I open up the floor to students and just let them ask whatever they want.

And yes, you get some funny ones. I get a lot of dinosaur questions, and some interesting ones about Adam and Eve, and those can be fun. You can play around with those a little bit and have some fun with it. But at the same time, some really good and profound questions will come up, and the advantage to that is that if one student asks a question and another student is afraid to ask that same question, the student who was afraid gets their question answered. That can be an incredibly important and powerful tool.

paragraphs.heading: Prepare your small group leaders
paragraphs.text: So I would encourage you to maybe do that this week, or to find a way to incorporate many questions into your large group time. Then, during small group time, you can drill those questions down a little bit deeper. But make sure, as you do that, that your small group leaders are adequately prepared to handle some of the questions. Based on your situation and the leadership you have in place and the volunteers you have in place, just make sure that they are equipped to properly answer. And remind them that it's okay if they don't have an answer — to say, "I don't have an answer," and to write those questions down, bring them back, and find a way to get those questions answered specifically.

paragraphs.heading: This week's storyteller
paragraphs.text: Another important, powerful tool is your storyteller this week. To have somebody in front of your students who has actually expressed doubt and walked through it in some way, shape or form can be incredibly important. That story, whatever they've been through, will resonate, I'm sure, with many of your students. So make sure you know that you don't need to find the best story or the biggest story or the most compelling story — just something that lets students see, "Hey, I'm not the only one going through this. I'm not the only student dealing with this. I'm not the only person who has ever dealt with this, and people have gotten through it."

paragraphs.heading: God can handle it
paragraphs.text: Because some students might just have little questions here and there. Other students might be at a significant crisis of faith in their lives, where they need serious direction. And after all that you've gone through in this study, some of those things may start to come up to the surface a little bit. So remind your students that no matter their questions, no matter their doubts, God can handle it, and that He has given us everything we need to be entirely confident of who He is, who Jesus is, and what our salvation means.

paragraphs.heading: Final week, final lesson
paragraphs.text: All right, you did it. This is the final week, the final lesson of this incredible year of studying apologetics and preparing your students to be one step closer to being entirely confident — to walk across the stage of graduation and to engage their culture with the truth of the gospel. I can't express how excited I am to hear the stories of our students and what they've been able to experience, and the stories of students who started off with skepticism and doubt and have been brought along into committed followers of Christ, proclaiming the gospel far beyond the walls of your youth group. So I'm excited, and I hope you're excited too.

There are just a couple of quick things I want to bring to your attention and talk through as you prepare. First and foremost, I hope you are preparing to celebrate. This has probably been some of the most difficult topics some of your students have ever dealt with in church, and that's awesome — that makes me very, very excited. So take the time to celebrate.

paragraphs.heading: Take an inventory
paragraphs.text: The second thing is to take some time to do an inventory. Go back to when you first started talking, and go back to where your students were. Have your students go back to where they were, and invite them to think it through: what was I thinking back then? Have them go back to their notes. What were you thinking in lesson 1.1 versus how you're thinking now, when the concept of apologetics was first introduced? The questions you had way back in the beginning — have those questions been answered now? What further questions do you have? Where do we go from here? How do we continue to move on?

For your seniors, ask them if they feel like they're ready. And if they're not, maybe ask them what you can do to help them be further ready for the next step — the next step in their lives, whether it be military, whether it be college, whether it be a gap year, whatever it is. What is next for them?

paragraphs.heading: Successes and failures
paragraphs.text: The next thing is successes and failures. For your storyteller, you want someone who can tell a great story about sharing the truth. But keep this in mind: you don't necessarily want somebody who successfully shared the gospel every time. Students are going to need to see some examples of falling flat on their face, because they probably are going to, and that's okay. Maybe that's a good thing, because you generally learn a lot more from failure than you do from successes. So have somebody who can express both sides, especially if you can find somebody who failed, learned from that failure, and moved on to some success.

paragraphs.heading: God gives the growth
paragraphs.text: Keep in mind, and remind your students time and again, that it's not us who does the saving. It is God's job. I have an analogy I've often given students: they're all going to be in different places, and God is going to have all different kinds of roles for them. Some water, some plant, but it's God who causes the growth. And I often talk about the wide range of jobs, from excavation to tree shaking.

I have a pastor friend of mine that I call a tree shaker, because he's one of those guys who is just so eloquent and so good at talking about the gospel that I think he can just say "bless you" and people come to faith in Jesus. He's just so good. God has gifted him in amazing ways. So I call him a tree shaker. He walks up to the tree that has been ripened by a bunch of work from a bunch of other people, and he gets up there and shakes that tree, and the fruit just falls.

That may be the gifting of some of your students, but that's not necessarily the gifting of all of your students. I typically call myself an excavator. I'm the guy who just messes people up and gets the land ready to be planted, who gets them all confused and thinking, and gets people ready to hear truth and understand what truth is. It could be all over the map.

paragraphs.heading: Encourage your students
paragraphs.text: So just remember to encourage your students that wherever they are on that spectrum, to be faithful to the gifts and talents God has given them. They are going to face some challenges. They are going to face questions they don't have answers to all the time, and they're going to have to seek those answers out. They are also going to have awesome success, and they're going to get the thrill of leading someone to know Christ.

paragraphs.heading: Tell us your stories
paragraphs.text: And remember, we continue to pray for you. We continue to work really hard here back at the home office to provide you with the best possible resources for you to disciple your students. Like I said, we would love to hear your stories. We would love to hear how this study has impacted you and impacted your students. Share them on Facebook, share them on Twitter and Instagram. Give us an email, give us a phone call — whatever it takes, let us know how this study has impacted you and impacted your students in your ministry.
